About This Document 
This document is supplied as a part of GE’s e-terrasource product. 
Purpose of This Document 
This document presents the “big picture” that describes how to build the following models 
in e-terrasource: 
• e-terrahabitat 
– Alarm model (ALARM) 
• e-terraplatform 
– Network model (NETMOM) 
– Contingency model (CTGS) 
– Remedial action scheme model (RASMOM) 
– Dynamic ratings model (DYNRTG) 
– SCADA model (SCADAMOM) 
– Generation model (GENMOM) 
– Generation alarm model (RGALM) 
– Hydro pond model (HYMOM) 
– Reserve monitor model (RESMOM) 
– Dispatcher Training Simulator model (DTSMOM) 
– Dynamics model (DYDEF) 
– Tagging model (TAGGING) 
– Safety model (SAFETY) 
• e-terracomm 
– Open Access Gateway model (OAGMOM) 
Each modeled object is described with regards to its purpose and usage by applications. If 
the object has any modeling variants, those are discussed as well. 
This document does not describe how to use the e-terrasource user interface in any detail. 
For more information, refer to the e-terrasource User’s Guide. 
This document also avoids field-by-field descriptions because that information is available 
on the user interface as tool tips on property sheets. Rather, this document presents more 
high-level information about the objects in the model and how they are used in various 
modeling scenarios. 
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page xxvi 
Who Should Use This Document 
This document is intended for users of e-terrasource who are responsible for building and 
maintaining models. These users are generally those whose routine duties are as a 
SCADA/EMS engineer. 
Non-traditional users can also benefit from this document. These users may be planners, 
operations technical specialists, operations trainers who have e-terrasimulator 
responsibilities, or real-time support staff whose background is predominantly in 
operations. 
Users are expected to have a technical understanding of creating models. All users are 
expected to have an understanding into the workings of their local power system and the 
operations of an interconnected power system. 
Structure of This Document 
This document is structured in the following manner: 
• Chapter 1 provides an overview of modeling in e-terrasource, and information and tips 
on getting started. 
• Chapter 2 provides information about network modeling. 
• Chapter 3 provides information about generation modeling. 
• Chapter 4 provides information about SCADA modeling. 
• Chapter 5 provides information about simulation modeling. 
• Chapter 6 provides information about alarm modeling. 
• Chapter 7 provides information about e-terracomm modeling. 
• Chapter 8 provides information about tagging modeling. 
For More Information 
For more information about e-terrasource, refer to the following: 
• e-terrasource Release Notes 
• e-terrasource Software Installation and Maintenance Guide 
• e-terrasource User’s Guide 
• e-terrasource Metamodel Guide

e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
1. Overview 
1.1 Why e-terrasource? 
The e-terrasource solution provides facilities to help you maintain a high-quality, consistent 
model. Although the primary assumption is that e-terrasource provides models for an 
Energy Management System (EMS) or SCADA system, it can be extended and configured to 
provide models for other systems, such as Market Management Systems (MMS), or virtually 
any system requiring a model. 
The e-terrasource solution facilitates efficiency in performing modeling tasks. This is 
accomplished by mechanisms such as: 
• Supporting multiple independent working environments (workspaces) 
• Allowing users to organize model changes into projects with effective dates 
Projects can easily be rescheduled and included or excluded from upcoming model 
releases. 
• Allowing large models to be broken into pieces (regional model authority sets) 
• Providing a variety of user interfaces suited to the task at hand, such as: 
– Modeling connectivity using Graphic Modeler schematic views 
– Bulk modeling using grid views or Microsoft Excel 
– Hierarchical exploration of models using tree views and property sheets 
– Graphically visualizing models of curves 
– Providing linkage displays tailored to quickly create relationships between records 
1.2 Model Overview 
The model schema supported by e-terrasource is entirely configurable. However, the 
standard product installation starts with the electrical network model schema defined by 
the International Electrotechnical Commission’s (IEC) Common Information Model (CIM) and 
extends it to support the following Energy Management System models: 
• e-terrahabitat 
– Alarm model (ALARM) 
• e-terraplatform 
– Network model (NETMOM) 
– Contingency model (CTGS) 
– Remedial action scheme model (RASMOM) 
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 2 Overview 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
– Dynamic ratings model (DYNRTG) 
– SCADA model (SCADAMOM) 
– Generation model (GENMOM) 
– Generation alarm model (RGALM) 
– Hydro pond model (HYMOM) 
– Reserve monitor model (RESMOM) 
– Dispatcher Training Simulator model (DTSMOM) 
– Dynamics model (DYDEF) 
– Tagging model (TAGGING) 
– Safety model (SAFETY) 
• e-terracomm 
– Open Access Gateway model (OAGMOM) 
The transformation subsystem of e-terrasource is responsible for converting the 
e-terrasource model to the various target models listed above. 
1.3 HTML Documentation 
Documentation of the model schema can be produced in HTML form. For information about 
exporting metamodel HTML documentation, refer to the e-terrasource Metamodel Guide.

detailed information about the entity and its properties and relationships.

1.4 Initializing e-terrasource 
If you intend to build a new model from scratch, you may choose to start by importing the 
e-terraplatform “newcase” savecases. In most cases, you probably have an existing model 
that you want to load into e-terrasource to initialize it. It is not unusual to refine and repeat 
the initialization process several times. However, once e-terrasource has been initialized 
with the desired model, it is expected that model maintenance will be performed in 
e-terrasource and models will be exported to e-terraplatform or other systems. 
This section discusses several mechanisms for loading an initial model into e-terrasource: 
• Importing e-terrahabitat Hdb models, either from an e-terramodeler archive or from 
Hdb clones or savecases 
• Importing a CIM/XML file 
• Loading data into the workspace RDBMS tables through other mechanisms 
• Loading data into the workspace using the Excel Import or CSV Import features 
If needed, you can use more than one of these mechanisms. For example, you might load 
EMS models from Hdb clones, and supplemental model information can be loaded from 
CIM/XML files or loaded directly into workspace tables via SQL scripts or CSV Import. 
The following sections provide additional details and advice on how to initialize 
e-terrasource using these approaches. 

 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 4 Overview 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
1.4.1 Importing from Hdb 
It is expected that many customers already have a model of their system in the form of a 
collection of Hdb savecases. Customers that used e-terramodeler have archives; an 
“archive” is simply a zipped collection of files, including savecases. 
To initialize e-terrasource from a set of Hdb savecases, the following information is of 
critical importance: 
• Before importing, ensure that the default model authority set type on the e-terrasource 
toolbar is set to the model authority set type that you want all of the new records to be 
assigned to. By default, the import sequences reference the model authority set type 
assignment specified on the toolbar. After import, they can be split into different model 
authority set types if desired, but the initial import must assign all records to a single 
model authority set type. Note that if you are re-importing data that was previously 
imported, the previous model authority set type assignment for the imported records is 
retained by default. For more information, refer to the 
“import_export_update_existing_mastype_assignments” parameter in the 
e-terrasource Software Installation and Maintenance Guide. 
• Ensure that you have the desired workspace open. The import operation does not reset 
the workspace before importing, so you should reset the workspace, if appropriate. In 
particular, if any previous import failed, there may be a partial data set in your 
workspace, so resetting it is advisable. 
• The correct savecases should be loaded into a set of clones with the same family name. 
The default family name is “MODEL”, and the application names are NETMODEL, 
SCADAMDL, GENMODEL, ALARM, DTSMODEL, TAGGING and OAGMODEL. 
• The Hdb models must be valid and free of errors. This validation should be performed by 
running the appropriate validation program (e.g., SMVERIFY, NETVALID, GMDRIVER, etc.). 
• The Hdb models must be properly cross-mapped. The cross-mapping is performed by 
validation programs such as SCADAMAP and GMDRIVER. 
• The Hdb models must be imported together in a single import sequence. This 
requirement is mandatory because the transformation process must “federate” the 
model during import. The term “federate” refers to the creation of a single e-terrasource 
record, even though that record may be represented in several e-terraplatform 
databases. The federation relies on name matching, as well as the use of SCADA (SCAPI) 
keys to identify linked records. For example, if the transformation process is unable to 
properly link records, this can result in the creation of Generic Equipment rather than 
the proper equipment type. 
• Records from e-terraplatform are expected to have stable Hdb object identifiers (OIDs) 
with no duplicates across any Hdb databases. During import, the Hdb OIDs are used as 
the CIM MRIDs, which leads to duplicate OIDs causing import errors. If the OIDs change, 
the records are treated as new records and new e-terrasource MRIDs are generated. If 
new e-terrasource MRIDs are generated for records that are really the “same” record, 
your projects may now have change items that cannot be applied because they 
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 5 Overview 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
reference old MRIDs. Use the “find_duplicate_oids” tool (described in the e-terrasource 
Software Installation and Maintenance Guide) to locate and correct any duplicate OIDs 
across all databases that are being imported into e-terrasource. For important 
information about how records are uniquely identified, see section 1.4.1.3 OIDs, CIM 
MRIDs, and e-terrasource MRIDs. 
• Generally speaking, there may be discrepancies if you perform a comparison between a 
source e-terraplatform savecase and a savecase exported from e-terrasource. For 
example, when importing a contingency model, only valid contingencies are imported 
into e-terrasource. For more information, refer to the e-terrasource Release Notes. 
Before initializing e-terrasource, you can globally configure the versions of e-terrahabitat, 
e-terraplatform, e-terrascada, and e-terracomm that are supported by your environment 
in the Administration Explorer’s Parameters grid. Set the values for the hdb_version, 
emp_version, scada_version, and comm_version, respectively, as shown in Figure 3. These 
parameters are, by default, used to determine the product versions when performing 
imports and exports. 
 
Figure 3. Select Product Versions 
Furthermore, you can specify the Hdb family name to use for imports and exports on the 
user’s property sheet. 
The initialization process is performed by clicking the Import button on the toolbar and 
choosing “Import into Workspace”. Then, choose the import sequence titled “EMS Import –
 All”, and click Next. The following dialog box is shown: 

 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 6 Overview 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
 
Figure 4. EMS Import Sequence 
Three types of operations are performed: 
• Dump each database using hdbexport. 
• Run the transformations to convert the Hdb models to a CIM/XML representation. 
• Import the CIM/XML into e-terrasource. 
The first type of operation is to dump the data from an Hdb clone to a CSV file using the 
hdbexport utility. This operation is performed for each of the supported databases, 
although a particular database can be skipped by unchecking the check box next to it. If 
you click the Edit button for a particular database, a dialog box is displayed that allows you 
to change the default parameters for the dump operation. 

 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 7 Overview 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
 
Figure 5. Dump Parameters 
If you change any parameter values, the new settings are retained in your user preferences. 
You can return to the default values by clicking the Restore Defaults button in the top right 
corner. 
After the data is dumped from the clones to CSV files (this includes performing the “reset –o” 
operation to initialize any null OIDs), the next step (“Transform All to CIM/XML – EMS”) is to 
execute the transformation process to read the CSV files and produce a CIM/XML file for 
import into e-terrasource. For further details about the transformation subsystem, refer to 
the e-terrasource Programmer’s Guide. 
The settings for the transformation step are shown below. The import file names shown 
here should match the file names from the Dump Parameters dialog box shown in Figure 5. 

 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 8 Overview 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
 
Figure 6. Transformation Parameters

1.4.1.3 OIDs, CIM MRIDs, and e-terrasource MRIDs 
Before initializing e-terrasource from Hdb, it is very important to understand the 
significance of Hdb OIDs in the import process. 
The import process uses Hdb OIDs to uniquely identify records. If you used e-terramodeler, 
it also required unique OIDs, so there are no particular concerns in this regard. However, if 
you did not use e-terramodeler, your OIDs may not be unique. As a form of protection 
during the import process, the hdbrio “reset -o” operation is performed to initialize null OIDs 
with unique values. 
If you are importing from CSV files rather than clones, the “reset -o” operation is not 
performed, so you should ensure that the CSV files were dumped from clones that had 
unique OIDs. 
It is also critical that there are no duplicate OIDs across all databases that are imported into 
e-terrasource. Prior to importing, use the “find_duplicate_oids” tool (described in the 
e-terrasource Software Installation and Maintenance Guide) to locate and correct any 
duplicate OIDs. 
For any given Hdb record, the OID should not change from import to import. This is because 
the Hdb OID is used as the unique identifier (RDF ID) in the CIM/XML file. As shown in Figure 
8, an e-terrasource MRID and a CIM MRID are generated to correspond to the record’s OID. 
The MRID-to-OID mapping is internally retained so that on subsequent imports, 
e-terrasource will use the same MRID when it encounters a record with the same OID. 
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 14 Overview 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
 
Figure 8. OID Usage During Import 
On the first import, new e-terrasource MRIDs are generated, but on subsequent imports, 
the same Hdb record with the same OID should have the same CIM MRID and e-terrasource 
MRID. It is important for the e-terrasource MRIDs to be the same because of projects that 
change the model reference records using the e-terrasource MRID. For this reason, it is 
preferable if the source savecases have valid, stable OIDs; otherwise, the “reset -o” 
operation assigns different values to records with null OIDs each time the import is 
performed. 
When importing from savecases, the CIM MRID is initialized to an RFC 4122 compliant 
representation of the e-terrasource MRID (it is the same hexadecimal numeric value with 
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 15 Overview 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
four dashes included). Although CIM MRIDs are editable on the e-terrasource UI, keep in 
mind that e-terrahabitat expects CIM MRIDs to be in RFC 4122 form. 
WARNING: e-terrasource exports OIDs with value “0” in the CSV export files. The OID fields 
are thus assigned a new random value in the clones and savecases. This is done by the 
hdbimport process during export every time you export from e-terrasource back out to 
Hdb. You should not import those savecases back into e-terrasource because the OIDs 
will not be consistent with the OIDs in the original import. The e-terrasource MRIDs will be 
different. This can be mitigated by using the Save_CSMMRID.sql and Restore_CSMMRID.sql 
sample scripts to revert back to the original MRIDs where possible. 
1.4.2 Importing a CIM/XML File 
The e-terrasource model can also be initialized by importing a CIM/XML file. This option is 
typically used when importing a model from another vendor system. Although this type of 
import does not provide all the data needed by e-terraplatform, it should provide the bulk 
of the power system model as a starting point. 
Upon installation, e-terrasource supports specific versions of CIM, as identified by a CIM 
“profile” name. The CIM profile named “ETS” is a special profile used for CIM/XML model 
exchange with e-terraplatform via the transformation subsystem. 
When a CIM/XML file is imported, the CIM MRIDs (also known as “RDF IDs”) are loaded into 
the e-terrasource records. If this is the first import of a CIM/XML file, a new e-terrasource 
MRID is generated for each record; otherwise, the CIM MRID for a record is used to look up 
the previously assigned e-terrasource MRID. This ensures that stable CIM MRIDs result in 
stable e-terrasource MRIDs. 
An example of a CIM MRID (RDF ID) in a CIM/XML file is shown here: 
<cim:Substation rdf:ID="_56B490DCDE440D1FE04014AC92606106"> 
   <cim:IdentifiedObject.name>CHENAUX</cim:IdentifiedObject.name> 
</cim:Substation> 
The initialization process is performed by clicking the Import button on the toolbar and 
choosing “Import into Workspace”. Then, choose the import sequence titled “CIM/XML 
Import”, and click Next. If you click the Edit button in the next dialog box, the following 
dialog box is shown: 
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 16 Overview 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
 
Figure 9. CIM/XML Import Parameters 
This dialog box lets you: 
• Choose either a file on your local PC or the e-terrasource server 
• Specify the file name 
• Specify the model authority set type to assign the imported records to 
• Specify the CIM profile used to process the file 
When e-terrasource is installed, several profiles are included by default: 
• CIM-R12: The CIM Common Power System Model (CPSM) profile, also known as the IEC 
61970-452 profile for CIM version 12. 
• CIM12-NETVALID: The CIM-R12 profile augmented with additional information that 
allows two e-terrasource systems to exchange network models that should pass 
e-terraplatform network validation. 
• CIM-R13: The CIM Common Power System Model (CPSM) profile, also known as the IEC 
61970-452 profile for CIM version 13. 
• CIM-R15-Equipment: The Equipment (EQ) profile for CIM version 15. 
• CIM-R15-DiagramLayout: The Diagram Layout (DL) profile for CIM version 15. It is used 
only for exchanging graphical layout information. 
• ETS: This profile is used to import and export models to e-terraplatform. 
• ETS-ModelNavigation: This profile is used to produce a CIM/XML file that contains only 
the data needed by the Model Navigation Service. 
When the import completes, your workspace should be populated with data from the 
CIM/XML file. It is advisable to save the workspace contents to a model authority set and 
then spend some time reviewing and validating the model to determine if re-importing is 
warranted for any reason. Details regarding the import processing, as well as detailed error 
messages, can be found in the log file for the CIM/XML Import/Export service on the 
e-terrasource server. For more information, refer to the e-terrasource Software Installation 
and Maintenance Guide. 

 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 17 Overview 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
Keep in mind that e-terrahabitat expects CIM MRIDs to be in RFC 4122 form. If you import 
data from a source that does not have RFC 4122 compliant CIM MRIDs, you can use the 
Nullify_CIMMRIDs.sql sample script to nullify all CIM MRIDs. In this case, e-terrasource will 
replace the null MRIDs with the RFC 4122 representation of the e-terrasource MRID. 
1.4.3 Directly Loading Workspace Tables 
A clear benefit of using a commercial Relational Database Management System (RDBMS) is 
that there are a tremendous number of tools that can be used to populate data into the 
workspace tables. The possibilities are endless, but before starting down this path, it is 
imperative that you refer to the “Tips and Tricks” chapter of the e-terrasource Software 
Installation and Maintenance Guide for information about using SQL in a workspace. 
1.4.4 Microsoft Excel/CSV Import 
While it may not be practical to completely initialize the e-terrasource model via the Excel 
import or CSV Import feature, it is certainly viable for populating selected tables. For 
information about modeling in Excel and CSV Import, refer to the e-terrasource User’s 
Guide. 
1.4.5 Initialize Domain Sets for e-terraplatform Version 
Most data validation performed during workspace validation is common regardless of the 
e-terraplatform version. However, there is a small subset of validation that is version 
dependent. If you are running workspace validation for a specific e-terraplatform system 
version, some domain sets may need to be disabled to support successful workspace 
validation. 
1. From the e-terrasource View menu, select “User Preferences”. 
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 18 Overview 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
2. From the User Preferences dialog box, click the “Change” button. 
 

 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 19 Overview 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
3. In the Change Domain Set Preferences dialog box, deselect entries that are specific to 
other versions of e-terraplatform and e-terrahabitat, and then click OK to preserve 
these settings as a user preference. 
 
1.5 Exporting to e-terraplatform 
One of the main purposes of e-terrasource is to supply models to e-terraplatform. Although 
the details regarding target environments (e.g., test vs. production) and modeling business 
processes may vary widely from organization to organization, the basic concept is the 
same: extract a portion of the model from e-terrasource, transform it, and place it into an 
e-terraplatform Hdb database. Imports into e-terrasource simply work in the opposite 
direction. 

 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 20 Overview 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
The following e-terraplatform models are supported by e-terrasource: 
Hdb Database Description 
ALARM e-terrahabitat alarm model 
CTGS e-terratransmission contingency analysis model 
DTSMOM e-terrasimulator simulation model 
DYDEF e-terrasimulator dynamics default model 
DYNRTG e-terratransmission dynamic ratings model 
GENMOM e-terrageneration generation model 
HYMOM e-terrageneration hydro pond model 
NETMOM e-terratransmission network model 
OAGMOM e-terracomm model 
RASMOM e-terratransmission remedial action scheme model 
RESMOM e-terrageneration reserve monitoring model 
RGALM e-terrageneration alarm model 
SCADAMOM e-terrascada SCADA model 
TAGGING Tagging model  
SAFETY e-terrascada SAFETY model 
 
Upon installation, e-terrasource is configured with several export sequences that are useful 
for exporting models to e-terraplatform. Each sequence has three basic steps: 
1. Produce CIM/XML that represents the data model in the workspace. 
The CIM/XML Import/Export service creates the CIM/XML using a CIM profile called “ETS”. 
The file is either a complete model representation (*.ets) or a partial representation 
(*.etspartial), depending on the chosen export sequence. Choosing “EMS Export Affected 
Domains” creates a partial file. 
2. Feed the CIM/XML data to the transformation subsystem and produce data that can be 
loaded into an Hdb database. 
For each supported Hdb database, the transformation subsystem has modules that 
contain instructions on how to convert the e-terrasource data into Hdb data (and vice 
versa for imports). 
3. Load the resulting Hdb data into a clone or savecase. 
Optionally, e-terraplatform validation programs can be executed, and the savecases 
can be compressed into a zip archive. 
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 21 Overview 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
The following EMS export sequences are configured when e-terrasource is installed. The 
sequences available on your system may vary from this list. 
 
EMS Export Sequence Description 
EMS Export – All Export CIM/XML, run transformations for each 
e-terraplatform model, and run validation. If 
successful, a zip archive is created. 
EMS Export – <database> Export CIM/XML, run transformation and 
e-terraplatform validation for the specified database. 
EMS Export Affected Domains Export CIM/ XML only for the Hdb databases impacted 
by the projects loaded in the workspace. Transforms 
and runs e-terraplatform validation for the impacted 
Hdb databases only. 
 
Note that individual steps in a sequence can be skipped by unchecking the step in the Edit 
Workspace Export Targets dialog box. 
The zip archive produced by the “EMS Export – All” sequence is intended to be used by the 
e-terraplatform DBSEQ (database sequence) utility. 
The e-terrasource database has no concept of a maximum number of records per table, 
such as the “MX” concept in e-terrahabitat Hdb databases. Therefore, e-terrasource allows 
you to model records beyond the limits of any Hdb MX values. If the exported data set 
exceeds the MX value for any record, the export process reports an error when attempting 
to load the data into the Hdb clone. If this occurs, you must increase the record’s MX value 
in Hdb or reduce the number of records in e-terrasource. 
By default, exports to Hdb are configured to use an Hdb clone whose family name is the 
export family specified on the e-terrasource user property sheet. 
Before exporting, ensure that the default model authority set type on the e-terrasource 
toolbar is set to the model authority set type that you want to export. By default, the export 
sequences reference the model authority set type assignment specified on the toolbar. 
The following sections describe the export steps and parameters for the primary 
e-terraplatform export sequences.

1.5.2 EMS Export – <database> 
There are several export sequences that are very similar, differing only in the database that 
is exported. These include the CTGS, DYNRTG, OAGMOM, RASMOM, RESMOM, SAFETY, and 
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 27 Overview 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
TAGGING databases. This sequence is the same for each, assuming the <database> name 
is replaced with the selected sequence. 
The following are the export steps for this sequence with their associated parameters: 
• CIM/XML EMS Export – EMS 
Creates an intermediate CIM/XML file from data retrieved from the e-terrasource 
database.  
– Export File Name: The name of the intermediate CIM/XML file to be created. 
– Model Authority Set Type to export: Only retrieve data from the identified Model 
Authority Set Type(s) when retrieving data out of the e-terrasource database. 
– Profile name: The name of the CIM Profile to use for exporting the data. This is set to 
“ETS” and cannot be changed. 
• Transform CIM/XML to <database> – EMS 
Transforms the data from the intermediate CIM/XML file into the intermediate CSV file. 
– CIM/XML EMS Export File Name: The name of the intermediate CIM/XML file from 
which data is retrieved to perform the transformation. 
– <database> Export File Name: The name of the intermediate CSV file to create as an 
output of the transformation. 
– EMP Version: The installed version of e-terraplatform. 
• Load <database> – EMS 
Loads data from the associated intermediate CSV file into the specified clone (there is a 
separate entry for each database to be loaded). 
– Database: The name of the database where the data is to be loaded. 
– Application: The application name of the clone where the data is to be loaded. 
– Family: The family name of the clone where the data is to be loaded. 
– Schema: The correct version of the e-terraplatform, e-terracomm, or e-terrahabitat 
environment associated with the clone where the data is to be loaded.  
– <database> Export File Name: The name of the CSV file from which the data is to be 
retrieved. 
• Validate <database> – EMS or Verify <database> - EMS 
Runs the Hdb validator in the clone where the data was loaded. 
– Database: The name of the database to be validated. 
– Application: The application name of the clone to be validated. 
– Family: The family name of the clone to be validated. 
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 28 Overview 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
– Schema: The correct version of the e-terraplatform or e-terracomm environment 
associated with the clone to be validated.

1.6 Getting Started 
Although a more thorough discussion of the e-terrasource user interface is contained in the 
e-terrasource User’s Guide, there are some important fundamentals to consider before you 
start modeling. 
• You must have a workspace open, as indicated on the toolbar. Furthermore, if you 
intend to change any of the data in the workspace, you must be the “owner” of the 
workspace. 
• You must create one or more projects to save your model changes into. The project(s) 
must be in a state that is not locked. Your currently active project is indicated on the 
toolbar. 
Important: Remember that when you click Save, the model changes are saved to the 
project that is currently active. 
• You must set your Default Model Authority Set Type on the toolbar. When you add new 
records to the model, the new records are assigned to the default model authority set 
type (unless the active project specifies a model authority set type as well). 
1.7 Best Practices 
e-terrasource is designed to be a flexible and configurable tool, with many ways to create, 
review, and update data. As such, the flexibility open the possibility for using inefficient 
approaches when performing modeling tasks. There are many ways to streamline your 
work to save time. 
The following recommendations should be considered best practices for using 
e-terrasource. 
• The project-based design for managing model changes in e-terrasource provides the 
capability to control when and if model changes are implemented in a production 
system. However, this process depends on an assumption that someone has the 
functional role of Modeling Lead. In cases where a team of model editors are 
implementing model updates, it is necessary for someone to select the projects to be 
included in a model release and to test the integration of these model edits into the 
same model export. 
• Project Workflow 
– A naming convention for related projects is recommended to help coordinate work 
between different specialists. In an EMS, it is common to have a specialist in both 
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 44 Overview 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
SCADA and Network Application modeling. In this case, model updates implemented 
by one of the specialist will depend upon the model updates implemented by the 
other. 
– Users who create new projects should check for existing related projects. 
– When a project is “released” for use either in production or as a dependency that 
may be referenced by other modelers, the project should be Locked and not updated 
again. Any further corrections should be created in a different “related” project. 
• Project Scope 
– If model edits for multiple objectives are entered in a single project, you will lose the 
capability to control the release of these edits separately. Stated differently, if a 
model-correction and new equipment are modeled in the same project, you will 
have no choice but to release both functional updates together. 
– Make it a habit to create a new project for each new independent set of model 
changes.  
• Project Do’s and Don’ts for good multi-user workflow management 
– Do 
∗ Create a new project when starting new modeling. 
∗ Be mindful of adhering to established naming conventions. 
∗ Lock a project when you are done to prevent accidentally adding unrelated 
change items to the wrong project. 
∗ Run a full workspace validation after loading projects from other modelers. 
– Do not 
∗ Combine two or more independent jobs into one project. 
∗ Unlock a project for additional editing once it has been locked. Assume that 
someone else may have already loaded that project into their own workspace. 
– Ensure 
∗ That a project passes e-terraplatform validation before locking a project. 
∗ That databases outside of your discipline do not fail validation as a result of your 
project. If it does, alert the expert in that area. 
• Build your model in a logical order 
– Start by populating reference tables. Maintaining control over reference tables is 
important for ensuring consistency in your model. 
– Use the proper table to model the object. For example, if you know an object is a 
transformer, model it as a PowerTransformer rather than as generic SCADA 
equipment (Generic Equipment). 
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 45 Overview 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
– If different subsystems or domains are built by different users, use the User 
Preferences dialog box to show only the property groups relevant to the user’s task. 
• Avoid populating records from scratch 
– Use copy and paste, or clone on tree views, or graphic modeler views to copy similar 
records. 
– Use deep copy on tree views to copy a hierarchy of records. Most tree view records 
are configured to support deep copy. 
– You can create powerful parameterized templates to quickly create groups of 
related records. 
• Use the proper user interface for the job 
– For equipment connectivity modeling, use the Graphic Modeler. 
– For bulk changes, use the Search feature to display a grid of target records, and then 
select a range of cells and enter a value for the entire range. 
– When linking records together, see if there is a linkage display available on the 
toolbar to speed up the creation of linkages. If not, create your own by placing two 
grid displays side by side and dragging and dropping linkages. 
– For curve data, check the shape of the curve to ensure that it has the expected 
shape. 
– Use the Show References feature on tree views to obtain grid displays of records 
that “point” to the selected tree view record. 
– Use the Show Children feature on property sheets to display a grid of each type of 
child of the target record. 
• Hide data that is not relevant to your task. Options for hiding data include the 
following: 
– Close property groups and hide or re-order columns on grids. These changes will be 
persisted as a user-preference. 
– Use the Show OnlyRequired Fields option. 
– Use the Domain-Sets user preference setting to control presentation and validation 
based upon subsystem domains. 
– Use metadata editing capabilities to set default values appropriate to your needs, 
and also permanently hide presentation of undesired properties by setting the 
property’s sort order to 0. 
• Take advantage of keyboard shortcuts when possible 
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 46 Overview 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
• Consider using the CSV Import feature to automate input of model updates from 
external sources 
• Consider using PowerShell scripts to automate repetitive tasks 
• Create separate Hdb modeling clones for each e-terrasource modeler 
This allows each modeler to export models from their own e-terrasource workspace into 
their own independent e-terrahabitat modeling clones, without affecting other 
modelers. 
• Consider exporting to Excel, particularly if you want to send model snippets to 
non-users of e-terrasource, and receive model changes back from them. 
– From a grid view of a single table, right-click and choose Export to Excel. 
– From any tree view record (except GeographicalRegion and 
SubGeographicalRegion), right-click and choose Export to Excel. 
– After making changes in Excel, choose Import Changes from Excel on the toolbar’s 
Import button. 
1.7.1 Creating Effective Templates 
Templates can be a powerful tool for model building. By spending some time up front to 
create effective templates, you can potentially save yourself a tremendous amount of data 
entry each time a template is used. 
Effective templates have the following characteristics: 
• They can be used in a wide range of modeling scenarios.  
For example, it is preferable to create a single Switch template that can be used for all 
types of switching devices (circuit breakers, disconnects, etc.) regardless of their voltage 
level or the station/region/area to which they belong. This allows you to create and 
maintain fewer, smarter templates instead of a large number of templates that the user 
must choose from. 
• They reduce the amount of information the user must enter. 
An effective template should prompt the user to enter a few parameter values, and then 
use those values to derive the values of various properties. Templates should also 
contain static values that represent “normal” modeling scenarios so that the user only 
has to change the values for abnormal situations. 
• They perform lookups to connect to objects outside the template. 
The standard installation of e-terrasource includes many queries that can be used to 
look up records in reference tables and other places. This can also serve to reduce the 
amount of information the user has to enter after instantiating the template. 
• They enforce modeling conventions. 
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 47 Overview 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
By using approved, tested templates, you can bring uniformity and consistency to the 
model. 
Many lookup queries are provided upon installation of e-terrasource for use in templates. 
These queries search for a record by some identifier (typically the record’s EMS name) and 
return its MRID value. The table below lists the available queries upon installation. The third 
column lists the ID of the template parameter that the query expects.

2. Network Modeling 
The core of the e-terrasource model is a CIM-based electrical network model. The CIM 
model has been augmented so that it supports the following network models in 
e-terraplatform: 
• NETMOM: This is the main network database used by the e-terratransmission 
applications. 
• CTGS: This is an auxiliary database that contains contingency definitions used for 
contingency analysis. The contingencies in this model reference the equipment in 
NETMOM. 
• RASMOM: This is an auxiliary database for defining remedial action schemes. Similar to 
CTGS, it references equipment in NETMOM. 
• DYNRTG: This is an auxiliary database for defining dynamic rating models. Similar to 
CTGS, it references equipment in NETMOM. 
2.1 Network Displays 
Network modeling can be performed from several different types of displays, depending on 
the task at hand. 
2.1.1 Tree View Displays 
There are several tree view displays that are available for network modeling. Click Network 
on the toolbar to see the list of available tree views. 
 
Figure 10. Network Tree Views 

 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 53 Network Modeling  
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
2.1.1.1 Network Model 
This is the main tree view for network modeling. It starts at the GeographicalRegion level, 
and then descends through SubGeographicalRegions into Substations. Station equipment is 
generally organized under VoltageLevel records. Each equipment terminal, any associated 
SCADA measurements, operational limits, and simulation models are shown as well. 
 
Figure 11. Network Model Tree View 

 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 54 Network Modeling  
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
2.1.1.2 Connectivity 
This tree view hierarchically displays the equipment terminals that are connected to 
connectivity nodes. Generally speaking, the Graphic Modeler’s Substation Detail display 
provides a more user-friendly view of equipment connectivity. 
 
Figure 12. Connectivity Tree View 
2.1.1.3 Contingency 
This tree view displays: 
• Contingency groups and the contingencies that belong to them 
• Contingencies and the elements belonging to them 
 
Figure 13. Contingency Tree View 

 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 55 Network Modeling  
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
2.1.1.4 Schedules 
The Schedules tree view shows the various network schedules and curves. A schedule is 
simply a curve where the X axis represents time. Modeling schedules is more complex than 
modeling simple curves due to the definition of the repeating time ranges for which the 
schedule is active. Area Load Curve is a time-based schedule although the name is “curve”. 
More details about the various schedules can be found in later sections. 
 
Figure 14. Schedules Tree View 

 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 56 Network Modeling  
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
2.1.1.5 Remedial Action Schemes 
The remedial action scheme (RAS) application in e-terraplatform requires a model where 
each scheme is defined with its trigger conditions and its component stages that define 
protective actions. The modeling of the schemes is performed on the remedial action 
scheme tree view. 
 
Figure 15. Remedial Action Scheme Tree View 

 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 57 Network Modeling  
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
2.1.1.6 Network Monitoring Group 
Monitoring of the electrical network by e-terraplatform applications requires the definition 
of monitoring groups. Equipment can undergo default monitoring, or it can be assigned to a 
non-default monitoring group. Monitoring is based on violations of operational limits or 
phase angle differences. The Network Monitoring Group tree view is used to support 
monitoring of network equipment. 
 
Figure 16. Network Monitoring Group Tree View 
2.1.1.7 Equivalent Network 
This tree view is used to define equivalent networks and the branch and shunt devices 
within them. 
 
Figure 17. Equivalent Network Tree View 

 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 58 Network Modeling  
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
2.1.2 Table/Grid Displays 
Grid displays of the tables in the network portion of the model are accessible via the Tables 
Explorer. Click Tables on the toolbar to display the Tables Explorer and expand the Network 
tree node. The tables are organized into logical groupings. 
 
Figure 18. Network Grid Displays in Tables Explorer 
Click a table name to display a paged grid of all of the records in the table. The number of 
records shown per grid page is controllable through your user preferences. 

 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 59 Network Modeling  
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
 
Figure 19. Substation Grid Display 
Keep in mind that grid displays must be manually refreshed using the Refresh button  at 
the top of the grid. 
Rather than paging through an entire grid, it is typically more efficient to use the Search 
toolbar button to enter search criteria for the specific records that you are looking for. 
2.1.3 Graphic Modeler Displays 
Because one of the main purposes of the network model is to define how pieces of 
electrical equipment are connected to each other, several Graphic Modeler displays are 
available that make it much easier to model connectivity. These displays are automatically 
generated based on the information in the model, so they are useful for visualizing and 
verifying correct equipment connectivity. 
2.1.3.1 Substation Overview Display 
The Substation Overview display provides a high-level view of the Substations within a 
SubGeographicalRegion and the branches (such as ACLineSegments, SeriesCompensator, 
and EquivalentBranches) that connect them. The overview can optionally be overlaid on a 
map. This display is useful for ensuring proper AC line connections between substations, 
and as a general navigation aid. You can right-click on the upper-left corner of a Substation 
icon to display the detail for that substation. 
The Substation Overview display is accessible on the Network Model tree view by 
right-clicking on a SubGeographicalRegion node and choosing Graphic Modeler. 

 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 60 Network Modeling  
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
 
Figure 20. Substation Overview Display 
Import and export of Substation Overview displays using the CIM Diagram Layout (DL) 
profile is not currently supported. 
 

 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 61 Network Modeling  
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
2.1.3.2 DC Line Overview Display 
 
Figure 21. DC Line Overview Display 
The DC Line Overview display shows substations containing DC equipment as well as 
DCConverters, DCLineSegments, VoltageSourceConverters, and the DC-type 
ConnectivityNodes to which they are connected. This display is useful for ensuring proper 
DC equipment connections. 
The DC Line Overview display is accessible on the Network Model tree view by right-clicking 
on any GeographicalRegion node and choosing Graphic Modeler. There is a single display 
for the entire model. 
Import and export of the DC Line Overview display using the CIM Diagram Layout (DL) 
profile is not currently supported. 
2.1.3.3 Substation Detail Display 
The Substation Detail display depicts the power equipment within a substation. 
Connections between the equipment terminals and AC-type ConnectivityNodes can be 
made. These displays are useful for adding new equipment, removing old equipment, and 
ensuring proper equipment connections. These displays also support easy navigation to 
neighboring substations. 
It is important to note that these displays use the topology information that is present 
exclusively in the network model. That is, it is based on network equipment terminals 
connected by ConnectivityNodes. 

 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 62 Network Modeling  
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
 
Figure 22. Substation Detail Display 
Station/VoltageLevel Assignment and Propagation 
As equipment records are dropped on to the canvas and connected, associations to the 
Substation or VoltageLevel are made as follows: 
• When a PowerTransformer is added on the GM canvas, its association to the parent 
substation is filled. 
• When equipment is added on the GM canvas, its Base Voltage and Equipment Container 
associations are initially empty.  When the equipment terminals are connected to a 
connectivity node, the voltage level assignment from the connectivity node propagates 
to the newly connected equipment. 
• You can right-click an equipment and choose Cascade VoltageLevel from the context 
menu to assign it to a different voltage level (or create a new one).  The assignment 
affects the Base Voltage and VoltageLevel assignment record for that equipment and all 
other equipment and nodes connected to it.  The cascade terminates when a 
transformer is reached or the equipment connects to another substation. 
ACLineSegment Connections 
In order to create an ACLineSegment connection between two substations, the 
ACLineSegment must have its Near Voltage Level and Far Voltage Level associations filled.  
For example, to create a new ACLineSegment between substations COBDEN and CHFALLS, 
you can do the following: 

 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 63 Network Modeling  
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
1. Open the Substation Detail display for COBDEN and use copy/paste or an 
ACLineSegment template to create a new ACLineSegment record. 
 
2. Connect one terminal to the desired bus  
 
3. Double-click the ACLineSegment to bring up its property sheet. In the Associations 
property group, set the Far Voltage Level to the desired VoltageLevel record in 
Substation CHFALLS.  
 

 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 64 Network Modeling  
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
4. Double-click the button to navigate to the CHFALLS Substation and locate the new 
ACLineSegment.  
 
5. Connect the open terminal to the desired bus.  
 
  

 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 65 Network Modeling  
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide

connections between them:

When importing/exporting a Substation Detail display using the CIM Diagram Layout 
profile, the following conventions are observed: 
• As a GE extension to the DL profile, the Diagram has an IdentifiedObject association that 
points to the Substation that the diagram depicts. On import, if this association is not 
provided then the GMDiagram record must be linked to the desired Substation manually 
after import in order to view it with graphic modeler. 
• For the records listed in Table 2 above: 
– A DiagramObject exists where the IdentifiedObject association references the record 
MRID.  For example, a DiagramObject representing a Switch has its IdentifiedObject 
association pointing to the Switch MRID. 
– The DiagramObject has one or more DiagramObjectPoint records to specify the x/y 
location of the record. For most DiagramObjects representing the records in Table 2 
a single DiagramObjectPoint is used, but ConnectivityNode and BusBarSection 
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 66 Network Modeling  
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
records may have two DiagramObjectPoints to represent opposite corners of a 
rectangle. 
• For connections between records listed in Table 2 above: 
– A DiagramObject exists where the IdentifiedObject association references the 
equipment terminal MRID that connects the equipment to the ConnectivityNode. For 
example, a DiagramObject representing a connection from a Switch to a 
ConnectivityNode has its IdentifiedObject association point to the MRID of the 
Terminal that connects the Switch with the ConnectivityNode. 
– Two or more DiagramObjectPoint records are exported to specify the x/y locations 
of the line ends. The sequenceNumber for the DiagramObjectPoints for a given 
DiagramObject are expected to be sequential and unique (e.g, 0, 1, 2, …). 
• For Records not listed in Table 2 above: 
– The records are not shown in the graphic modeler. On import, these DiagramObject 
records and their corresponding DiagramObjectPoints are created but not used. 
They may be discarded after graphic modeler is used to open and save the diagram. 
– No DiagramObjectStyle records are used by graphic modeler at this time.

There are two groups of operational limits: branch flow and voltage. For branch flow, there

2.2.2 Topology 
2.2.2.1 Geographical Region 
This represents a geographical region of a power system network model. It is mapped to

2.2.2.2 SubGeographical Region 
This represents a subset of a geographical region of a power system network model. It is 
mapped to the NETMOM DV class. 
2.2.2.3 Substations 
A substation is a collection of many components and measurements, such as a generator 
and its MW flow analogs. 
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 71 Network Modeling  
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
A substation is defined within a SubGeographicalRegion, and its name must be globally 
unique. Information about substations is used by all e-terraplatform subsystems: 
e-terratransmission, e-terrascada, e-terrageneration, and e-terrasimulator. 
2.2.2.4 Voltage Levels 
A voltage level represents a collection of equipment at one common system voltage 
forming switchgears. The equipment typically consists of breakers, busbars, 
instrumentation, controls, regulations, and protection devices as well as assemblies of all 
these. 
2.2.2.5 Line 
See section 2.2.3.1 AC Transmission Lines. 
2.2.2.6 Bay 
A bay is a collection of power system resources within a given substation that includes 
conducting equipment, protection relays, measurements, and telemetry. 
Equipment can be contained by bays, and this grouping can be found in the SCADA Model 
tree view as a special type of Equipment Group in e-terrasource. However, the Network tree 
view still relies on the voltage level container defined at each device, and the bay container 
is not included. The measurement definition for devices in e-terrasource is the same 
whether it is in a bay or not. 
In an EMS database, except for switches, bay information is not stored in NETMOM. Bay 
device measurements can be mapped by NETMOM, similar to non-bay devices, following 
the SCADA-NETMOM mapping rules. However, there is no network application available for 
the bay itself. 
2.2.2.7 Connectivity Nodes 
Connectivity nodes are points where terminals of conducting equipment are connected 
together with zero impedance. There are two kinds of nodes: AC or DC. Connectivity nodes 
are mapped to the NETMOM ND and DCND classes. 
2.2.2.8 Load Areas 
See section 2.2.4.3 Load Areas. 
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 72 Network Modeling

2.2.2.9 Company 
A company is a legal entity that owns and operates power system resources and is a party 
to interchange and transmission contracts. 
2.2.2.10 Company Resources 
A company can own or operate different resources, and a resource can belong to different 
companies.

2.2.3 Power System Equipment 
All power system equipment has one or more terminals. ACLineSegment, 
SeriesCompensator, EquivalentBranch, Switch, DCLineSegment and DCPole are “series” 
devices that have two terminals (a near terminal and a far terminal). Both DCConverter and 
VoltageSourceConverter have three terminals to connect to both the AC and the DC 
network. The other pieces of equipment are “shunt” devices and have only one terminal. 
Terminals are connected to ConnectivityNodes, which can be AC or DC nodes. 
The “Partial Model” flag is used to exclude equipment at distribution voltage levels from the 
RTNET solution, but to allow the energization status of the equipment to be computed. The 
flag is added to the following equipment: ACLineSegment, EquivalentLoad, 
SeriesCompensator, ShuntCompensator, StaticVarCompensator, Switch, 
SynchronousMachine, and TransformerWinding. To use this feature it is necessary to 
enable an RTNET solution option “Run Special Topology Processor after RTNET” which is the 
SPTOPRUN flag in SEMATRX. For more details, refer to the e-terratransmission 
documentation. 
2.2.3.1 AC Transmission Lines 
Each AC transmission line can contain one or more two-terminal ACLineSegments and/or 
SeriesCompensators. Each end of an ACLineSegment or SeriesCompensator must be 
assigned to a VoltageLevel within a substation. A zero impedance line is modeled as an 
ACLineSegment with the ZeroImpedanceLine flag set. 
Typically, series capacitors are placed in service on long EHV transmission lines. Their 
purpose is to add stability and allow increased power flows. These are modeled as 
SeriesCompensator devices, although they map to NETMOM LN records, just as 
ACLineSegments do. 
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 73 Network Modeling

A line is defined under a SubGeographicalRegion since it may connect different substations. 
The structure is as follows: 
 
Inside the substations, the ACLineSegments and SeriesCompensators are defined under the 
VoltageLevel associated with the near/from end. 
 
All the conductor parameters are in Ohms. ACLineSegment and SeriesCompensator should 
have positive resistance and conductance. Zero impedance lines should have zero 
resistance and conductance. 
For operational limit sets that can be applied to both ends, they can be defined directly

2.2.3.2 Equivalent Shunt/Branch/Network 
An equivalent network represents an external meshed network that has been reduced to an 
electrically equivalent model. EquivalentShunt records are used for one-terminal (shunt) 
models, and are mapped to the NETMOM EQLN class. EquivalentBranch records are used 
for two-terminal (series) models, and are also mapped to the NETMOM EQLN. 
The Equivalent Network has its own navigation tree but the terminals stay in the network 
model. 
2.2.3.3 Bus Bar Sections 
A BusBarSection is a conductor, or group of conductors, with negligible impedance that 
serves to connect other conducting equipment within a single substation. Voltage 
measurements are typically obtained from VoltageTransformers that are connected to 
BusBarSections. A bus bar section can have many physical terminals but, for analysis, it is 
modeled with exactly one logical terminal in e-terrasource. The modeling structure for a 
BusBarSection is shown below. 
 
In NETMOM, the nodes with a BusBarSection connected to them have the BSSECT flag set to 
True. 
More information about modeling SCADA measurements at a BusBarSection can be found 
in section 4.4.3 Measurements/Limits. 
2.2.3.4 Power Transformers 
A power transformer is an electrical device consisting of two or more coupled windings, 
with or without a magnetic core, for introducing mutual coupling between electric circuits 
at different voltage levels. Transformers can be used to control voltage and phase shifts 
(MW flow). The modeling structure for a transformer is shown below, with the 
TransformerWinding and its children records repeated for each winding. Two- and 
three-winding transformers are the norm. 
Substation 
   |-- VoltageLevel 
       |-- BusBarSection 
           |-- OperationalLimitSet 
           |-- Terminal 
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 75 Network Modeling  
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
 
Each winding can optionally have its own TapChanger, which defines the voltage/power 
regulation characteristics. 
SCADA measurements are directly defined under TransformationWinding (for more details, 
see section 4.4.3 Measurements/Limits). 
Simulation data is directly defined under TransformerWinding (for more details, see chapter 
5 Simulation Modeling). 
2.2.3.4.1 Two- and Three-Winding Transformers 
A two-winding transformer consists of primary (high side) and secondary (low side) 
windings. Typical applications are instances that only require transforming voltages up or 
down. An example is a generator step-up transformer. 
A three-winding transformer consists of primary (high side) and secondary (low side) 
windings and an additional tertiary winding. Typical applications are instances that require 
transforming voltages down from one transmission level to another and a third level via the 
tertiary winding. An example is a substation transformer that changes 345 KV voltage to 
230 KV voltage while the tertiary is connected as station service supply at 13.2 KV. The 
tertiary winding is also used for connecting reactive control devices. 
For a three-winding transformer, the EMS requires a pseudo node defined at the middle 
point. A connectivity node association is added to the PowerTransformer class to support 
that; this node is usually at the 1 KV level. 
A two-winding transformer must have identical EMSNames for the export To EMS to 
correctly export the windings as a single XF record in NETMOM. Power transformers with 
three or more Transformer Windings must have unique EMSNames under the power 
transformer for the export to EMS to correctly export the windings as each has its own XF 
record in NETMOM. All winding EMSNames (with exception for the primary and secondary 
windings belonging to the same two-winding power transformer) in a substation should be 
unique. 
If you would like to add a new two-winding transformer based on an existing one, the key 
step is to always manually update the Transformer Winding EMSNames immediately after 
creating them via deep copy and paste. e-terrasource workspace validation also provides 
Synchronize EMSName Validation and Network Terminal Name Autogeneration if needed. 
Winding parameters such as resistance and reactance are defined in Ohms; conductance 
and susceptance are defined in Siemens. Each winding has a winding type (primary, 
Substation 
   |-- PowerTransformer 
       |-- OperationalLimitSet 
       |-- TransformerWinding

           |-- TapChanger (including voltage and phase shifter) 
           |-- OperationalLimitSet

e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide

transformers, a “dummy” middle connectivity node is also defined. If transformers have 
delta connections, the parameters must be converted to the corresponding Y connection

2.2.3.4.2 TapChangers 
A transformer tap is a connection point along a transformer winding that allows a certain 
number of turns to be selected. By this means, a transformer with a variable turn ratio is 
produced, enabling voltage/power regulation of the output. The tap position is moved via a 
tap changer mechanism. 
Load tap changers (LTC) are usually used on the transmission system to modify system 
voltage/power. There are two basic designs: off-load and on-load. On-load tap changers 
(also called “Tap Change Under Load”, or TCUL) are utilized in circumstances where a supply 
interruption to effect a tap change is unacceptable. 
The LTC tap of a phase shifter is different from the LTC tap of a transformer, allowing the 
magnitude and phase angle to be adjusted independently. Thus, when both voltage and 
MW flow are being regulated, two physically different tap changers are present on the 
same transformer winding. 
There are two property groups for TapChanger: static and operational. Static parameters 
such as high/low steps are not related to the transformer winding operating conditions. 
Each transformer winding may or may not have a tap changer. If a tap changer exists, it 
can be fixed or adjustable. The fixed one has the same minimum and maximum tap 
positions, while the adjustable one has a range of tap positions with different minimum and 
maximum steps. 
There are also two types of tap changer depending on their regulation function: voltage or 
phase shifter. The tap changer can reference a time-based regulation schedule or a 

 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 77 Network Modeling  
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
load-based regulation schedule. The regulation node must also be specified. Remote 
control of a node that is in a different station from that of the transformer is supported. 
TapChangers with the same name should have the same static parameters since the EMS 
groups them together based on those parameters. 
When the tap changer position changes, the transformer impedance parameters should 
also be adjusted by the network applications (for more details, see section 2.3.2 Curves). 
Note: Currently, due to EMS restrictions, two transformers must be modeled if both 
voltage and power are regulated. 
2.2.3.4.3 Voltage Regulation 
In certain situations, such as for three-winding transformers, an unusual (nonlinear) 
relationship between tap setting and voltage tap ratio may exist. For these cases, tap ratio 
tables can be assigned to tap changers. Transformers assigned to that tap type have their 
voltage tap ratios calculated using the table. If no tap ratio table is assigned, transformers 
have their tap ratios calculated in the usual linear manner. 
2.2.3.4.4 Phase Shifter 
Phase-shifting transformers (PST) are used on the transmission system to alter impedance 
to force power to flow down a desired path. The main benefits of phase-shifting 
transformers are the protection of lines and transformers from thermal overload and an 
improvement of transmission system stability. They allow control of the power flow 
between different networks, for parallel long distance overhead lines or for parallel cables. 
Additionally, a phase-shifting transformer is very often the most economic approach to 
power flow management. 
The transformer/phase shifter impedance can optionally be modeled as a function of the 
phase shifter’s angle, in degrees. The correction table for phase-shifter impedance is 
referenced in the phase shifter’s tap changer. The correction table gives X and 
corresponding Y values, where X is the phase shift in degrees, and Y is multiplied by a phase 
shifter’s nominal impedance to obtain the corrected impedance. If an impedance correction 
table is not referenced, the phase shifter’s impedance is assumed to be constant. 
2.2.3.4.5 Operational Limit Set 
For two-winding transformers, if the operational limit sets apply to both primary and 
secondary windings, they can be defined directly under the parent power transformer. If the 
limits apply to only one side, the operational limit set needs to be modeled under the 
respective winding with the terminal association filled out. 
For three-winding transformers, the operational limit sets should always be defined under 
each winding. 
Alternate limits are also modeled as operational limit sets with the branch priority specified. 
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 78 Network Modeling  
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
2.2.3.5 DC Modeling 
High-voltage DC (HVDC) is used on the power system for various applications. Unlike AC 
transmission, which has higher losses when transmitting power, DC can be used to transmit 
power over long distances with very little loss. Also, the construction cost of a DC line is less, 
there are no power angle concerns, and right-of-way needs are lessened. 
DC transmission is most cost effective when used over long distances. 
There are disadvantages to DC, such as the inability to transform voltages, difficulty in 
tapping into HVDC lines, the complexity and expense of HVDC converters, and the fact that 
DC lines can be sources of strong harmonics. 
Another use of HVDC is to provide transfer paths between interconnections. This is 
accomplished by constructing back-to-back DC ties. DC stations are equipped with 
rectifiers, filter banks, line segments, inverters, and controllers. 
Another use of HVDC is to connect systems (interconnections) that operate at different 
frequencies — or, in the case of the United St ates, to connect interconnections that operate 
at different versions of the same frequency. This is the case of the Eastern, Western, and 
Texas Interconnections. In such instances, back-to-back HVDC converters are used. 
2.2.3.5.1 DCConverter 
A DCConverter is a type of bi-directional AC-DC conversion equipment that can be used to 
control DC current, DC voltage, DC power flow, or firing angle. The modeling structure for a 
DCConverter is shown below. 
 
Each DCConverter has two terminals connected to DC nodes and one terminal connected 
to an AC node. 
DC converters are modeled as station components. Each DCConverter consists of one or 
more bridges. The number of bridges in a converter can be changed online and impact the 
nominal voltage of the converter. Converter nominal voltage per bridge is entered during 
the modeling phase. 
Converters cannot control independently. The concept of regulation modes for individual 
converters does not apply. Regulation modes are applied to poles during the solution 
process, and solved pole voltage and current levels are distributed to converters within the 
pole. 
No distinctions are made in the modeling or the software between inverters and rectifiers, 
except when determining angle limits. Different limits are supported for firing angle and 
extinction angle. 
Substation 
   |-- VoltageLevel 
       |-- DCConverter 
           |-- Terminal 
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 79 Network Modeling  
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
The DC converter transformer model supports both two-winding transformers and a 
three-winding transformer model, with a synchronous condenser at the tertiary. For each 
converter, a single two- or three-winding transformer connects it to the AC network. 
Three-winding converter transformers are modeled as three two-winding transformers in a 
Y configuration, with only the primary tap being movable. This configuration also supports a 
synchronous condenser connected to the tertiary. 
Movable taps on converter transformers cannot be used to regulate any AC bus voltages, 
but they can be used to regulate DC voltage, current, or MW by controlling the AC voltage 
input to the converter. 
Only one set of converter current ratings is supported. 
2.2.3.5.2 VoltageSourceConverter 
A VoltageSourceConverter is a type of bi-directional AC-DC conversion equipment that can 
control its own MVAR injection into the AC bus, allowing it to regulate a local AC bus 
voltage. 
The modeling structure for a VoltageSourceConverter is shown below. 
 
Each VoltageSourceConverter has two terminals connected to DC nodes, and one terminal 
connected to an AC node. 
Voltage source converters are modeled as station components. Each 
VoltageSourceConverter consists of one or more bridges. The number of bridges in a 
converter can be changed online. 
Voltage source converters can be controlled independently to regulate either AC node 
voltage or MVAR injection. Regulated AC nodes for voltage source converters are defined in 
the modeling phase and must be in the same AC station as the converter. Voltage targets 
for local regulation are, by default, from schedules. Manual entries can be made to override 
the scheduled values. If a voltage-regulating voltage source converter violates a limit, the 
device is “type-switched” by fixing its MVAR output at the violated limit, and the bus voltage 
is allowed to solve unregulated. 
The voltage source converter transformer model may either be a two-winding or 
three-winding transformer. The VoltageSourceConverter does not control the tap. Tap 
position values may be manually entered or measured in the real-time environment. Firing 
and extinction angles are not modeled for the VoltageSourceConverter. 
Substation 
   |-- VoltageLevel 
       |-- VoltageSourceConverter 
           |-- Terminal 
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 80 Network Modeling  
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
2.2.3.5.3 DCPole 
DC pole has two terminal connections in the DC network: a single neutral connection, and a 
single “top” or “bottom” connection to one or more DC lines. Between its neutral connection 
and its DC line connection, a DC pole is modeled as a collection of DC converters in parallel, 
in series, or in both configurations. Within a pole, all series and parallel converter 
topological configurations are supported, including combinations of series and parallel 
converters. Topology changes can be made online by changing component node 
assignments. 
Unbalanced operation of bipoles is supported. There are no distinctions made in the model 
between “top” and “bottom” poles in a bipole, nor are there any restrictions against 
monopolar operation. 
Each pole regulates current, voltage, power, or firing/extinction angle, depending on its 
regulation mode. Poles regulate to their individual setpoints, which can be derived from a 
pole measurement (State Estimator only), from a schedule, or from its share of the DC 
controller’s setpoint. In the network model, each pole that is regulating power or current is 
assigned to one, and only one, DC controller. 
All poles in constant power mode must get their power setpoint from pole power 
measurement (State Estimator only), from their assigned DC controller, from their assigned 
MW schedule, or (optionally) from a user-entered override setpoint on the pole. If from a DC 
controller, the pole is assigned a portion of the DC controller’s power setpoint, based on the 
pole’s participation factor. 
Within the DC network solution software, all actual regulation is done at the pole level. 
Individual converters within a pole do not need to be assigned their own regulation 
setpoints or regulation modes, either by the user or internally by the software. At the 
solution, each converter’s solved voltage and current values are derived from its pole’s 
solved voltage and current values, distributed to converters based on converter topology 
within the pole. 
To avoid unsolvable or unrealistic problems, the following rules must be followed regarding 
the selection of regulation modes for DC poles: 
• In every DC circuit, there must be at least one pole that is regulating voltage or angle. 
However, multiple poles regulating voltage or angle cannot be connected in parallel 
(that is, to the same nodes). 
• Each pole that is regulating current or power must be a part of at least one loop in the 
DC circuit containing no other poles in that mode (a loop can include ground return). 
• In any pole that is regulating angle, and whose taps are discretely regulating voltage, all 
converter transformers in the pole must use the same tap model. That is, they must 
have the same nominal tap setting, the same tap step size, etc., since taps in this pole 
move together. This requirement applies only to poles regulating both angle and 
voltage. 
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 81 Network Modeling  
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
2.2.3.6 Generating Units and Synchronous Machines 
In electricity generation, an electric generator is a device that converts mechanical energy 
to electrical energy. The reverse conversion of electrical energy into mechanical energy is 
done by a motor. Motors and generators have many similarities. The source of mechanical 
energy can be a reciprocating or turbine steam engine, water falling through a turbine or 
waterwheel, an internal combustion engine, a wind turbine, a hand crank, compressed air, 
or any other source of mechanical energy. 
In e-terrasource, generators are modeled as GeneratingUnit and SynchronousMachine. The 
modeling structure is shown below. 
 
2.2.3.6.1 Physical (Individual) Units 
A synchronous machine is an electromechanical device that operates synchronously with 
the network. It is a single machine operating either as a generator or as a synchronous 
condenser or pump. Physical units are modeled as SynchronousMachines with different 
operating modes. 
In addition to the generation of electricity, generators are also used as a resource for 
voltage regulation. This is accomplished by changes in the excitation system voltage. These 
excitation changes set the generator to be either “leading” or “lagging”. This method raises 
transmission system voltage by “feeding” VARs to the system, or it lowers transmission 
system voltage by taking in VARs. This is accomplished simultaneously with the generation 
of real power. 
Line drop compensation is modeled to control the unit reactive power output to achieve a 
specified target voltage at a virtual location of specified percentage on step-up transformer 
reactance. 
This behavior is obtained by controlling the target voltage at the specified remote 
regulation bus using the following equation: 
VRegtarg = Vspec + (1 - X) (VLocal –Vremote) 
where: 
• Vspec: Specified target voltage magnitude of the generator (considered to be specified at 
the virtual bus) 
• X: Fraction of line drop compensation (the value should be between 0.0 and 1.0) 
provided for a given generator regulating a remote bus 
Substation 
   |-- GeneratingUnit 
   |-- VoltageLevel 
       |-- SynchronousMachine 
           |-- Terminal 
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 82 Network Modeling  
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
When X is 1.0, it regulates the local voltage. When X is equal to 0, it regulates remote 
voltage. 
• VLocal: Terminal voltage magnitude of the generator regulating a remote bus 
• Vremote: Actual voltage magnitude at the remote regulation bus 
2.2.3.6.2 Logical (Aggregated) Units 
For most cases, one generating unit contains one synchronous machine. Synchronous 
machines in condenser mode do not have a matching generating unit. In some 
circumstances, it may be necessary or desirable to represent several small generating units 
as one unit. Such an instance might be a wind farm consisting of many small rated turbines. 
In this case, the wind farm can be modeled as one unit. 
The output of the individual units is normally summed together at the source RTU, and the 
total generation is displayed on the EMS, DTS, and modeling system as a logical unit. 
2.2.3.6.3 Synchronous Condensers 
A synchronous condenser is a synchronous motor that is not attached to any driven 
equipment. Its field is controlled by a voltage regulator to either generate or absorb 
reactive power as needed to support a system’s voltage or to maintain a system’s power 
factor at a specified level. The condenser’s installation and operation are identical to large 
electric motors. 
A hydro generator can be “motored”, which basically turns it into a synchronous condenser. 
This process is accomplished by “blowing down” the water located in the scroll case, 
allowing the turbine to spin free. 
Increasing the device’s field excitation results in its furnishing magnetizing power (kilovars) 
to the system. Its principal advantage is the ease with which the amount of correction can 
be adjusted. The energy stored in the rotor of the machine can also help stabilize a power 
system during short circuits or rapidly fluctuating loads such as electric arc furnaces. Large 
installations of synchronous condensers are sometimes used in association with high 
voltage direct current converter stations to supply reactive power. 
More details about generation modeling can be found in chapter 3 Generation Modeling. 
SCADA measurements are directly defined under a synchronous machine or generating 
unit (for more details, see section 4.4.3 Measurements/Limits). 
Simulation data is directly defined under a synchronous machine (for more details, see 
chapter 5 Simulation Modeling). 
2.2.3.6.4 Unit_MVARCapCurve 
Single or multiple MVAR capability curves can be linked to each SynchronousMachine. The 
Unit_MVARCapabilityCurve table describes the many-to-many relationship. 
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 83 Network Modeling  
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
2.2.3.7 Switches 
A switch is a generic device designed to open or close one or more electric circuits. It can be 
a circuit breaker, a disconnector, a fuse, a ground disconnector, a jumper, or a load break 
switch, which can be specified as a switch type. The common electrical attribute of all such 
elements is that they are either open (infinite impedance) or closed (zero impedance). Each 
device is a branch whose relationship to the network components is identified by its two 
terminal branches. NETMOM has its own short names for switch types that are defined in 
e-terrasource as CBType. A switch schedule can be assigned to a switch if it has a schedule 
of operation that is a function of time. If not contained in a Bay, the EMSName of a switch 
must be unique within the same device type in a substation. For a Bay switch, the 
EMSName must be unique under the same bay.  
The modeling structure for a switch is shown below. 
 
SCADA measurements are directly defined under “Switch” (for more details, see section 
4.4.3 Measurements/Limits). 
Simulation data is directly defined under “Switch” (for more details, see chapter 5 
Simulation Modeling). 
Operational limit sets that can be applied to both ends can be defined directly under 
“Switch”. If the limits apply to only one end, operational limit sets need to be modeled under 
the respective terminal. Alternate limits are also modeled as operational limit sets with the 
branch priority specified. 
2.2.3.8 Shunt Compensators 
ShuntCompensators, including capacitors and reactors, are utilized on the power system by 
system operators to help regulate system voltage. Capacitors are inserted to raise 
transmission system voltage. Reactors are inserted to lower transmission system voltage. 
These devices can be configured for automatic or manual insertion. 
A ShuntCompensator is one-terminal equipment. The modeling structure for a 
ShuntCompensator is shown below.
