3.2.12 HostControlArea 
A host control area is defined in the EMS as an Automatic Generation Control (AGC) area. 
Host control areas are at the top of a hierarchical tree that is usually associated with the 
central business unit, the utility. At least one host control area must be designated as the 
EMS host control area. All other host control areas must be designated as non-EMS 
(external) areas. The HostControlArea class is mapped to the OPA record in GENMOM. 
Note: While not required, it is recommended that internal host control areas be ordered 
using the GenOrder property prior to external host control areas. 
Whenever you define a host control area, you need to define at least one generating unit so 
power exchanges can be represented and calculated properly by the e-terrageneration 
and e-terratransmission applications, which account for power transactions by adjusting 
unit output. In addition, you must define an area frequency measurement for the EMS host 
control area. 
Figure 43 illustrates the geographic alignment of the host control areas and operating 
divisions of a fictitious power and light company represented in the sample EMP60 model. 
The EAST host control area (with gray shading) contains one operating division, EAST. The 
WEST host control area (with dotted shading) contains two operating divisions, NORTH and 
SOUTH. The ECAR host control area belongs to another company. 
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 143 Generation Modeling 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
 
Figure 43. Geographic Alignment of Host Control Areas and Operating Divisions 
3.2.12.1 ACE Deadband and Control Regions 
Figure 44 shows how the Area Control Error (ACE) deadband and the various AGC control 
regions are defined. The deadband and control regions (regulation region indicator: RRI) are 
a function of the relative values of ACE and the integral of ACE. In addition, the ACE 
deadband is dynamic, being a function of time. 

 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 144 Generation Modeling 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
 
Figure 44. ACE Deadband and AGC Control Regions 
The dynamic attribute of the ACE deadband is used to adjust the effective deadband for 
AGC controls. As soon as ACE comes within the static deadband range, the dynamic 
deadband is increased to its maximum value, known as the “ACE emergency assist limit”. As 
long as ACE stays within the static deadband range, the dynamic deadband equals the 
emergency assist level. If ACE comes out of the static deadband range and stays out, the 
dynamic deadband gradually decays from the emergency assist level to the static 
deadband level. The rate of decay is a function of the analyst-entered dynamic deadband 
time constant, as Figure 45 illustrates. 

 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 145 Generation Modeling 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
 
Figure 45. ACE Deadbands and ACE Region Limits 
The dynamic ACE deadband is defined as follows: 
DACEDB = ACEDB + (DT/DTMAX) * (ACEEMN - ACEDB) 
where: 
• DACEDB is the dynamic ACE deadband. 
• ACEDB is the static ACE deadband defined in the database. 
• DT is DTMAX minus the time (in seconds) for which ACE has remained outside DACEDB 
(limited between zero and DTMAX). 
• DTMAX is the maximum time limit (in seconds) defined in the database. 
• ACEEMN is the emergency-assist ACE level defined in the database. 
Also: 
If the magnitude of ACE < ACEDB 
then: 
Set DT = DTMAX, or DACEDB = ACEEMN 
The integral of ACE is internally limited to a maximum value, whereas ACE itself is not. 

 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 146 Generation Modeling 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
3.2.12.2 Variable Frequency Bias Calculation 
Variable frequency bias (VFBIAS) predicts how much the MW output of a host control area 
changes for every 0.1 Hz of frequency variation that occurs in one AGC cycle. Valid values of 
VFBIAS reside between the variable frequency bias low limit (VFBMIN) and the high limit 
(VFBMAX). 
Variable frequency bias is calculated as follows: 
VFBIAS = FBLOAD + FBGEN 
where: 
• FBLOAD represents the Load Contribution and is calculated as follows: 
FBLOAD = LDBIAS /1000 * SLOAD 
where LDBIAS represents the Area Load Bias, and SLOAD represents the System Load. 
• FBGEN represents the Generation Contribution and is calculated as follows: 
FBGEN = DBV * DSK * SGVRES 
where DBV represents the Deadband Variable. DBV represents how the unit governors 
respond to the frequency deviation exceeding a threshold. 
DBV values reside between the unit contribution minimum (DBVMIN) and maximum 
(DBVMAX). 
The DSK term represents the Droop Scalar constant. This constant specifies how much 
of the generation frequency bias is applied to the area frequency bias. 
DSK is used to globally adjust the droop characteristics of all generators. DSK also 
models how the area’s unit governors respond to frequency deviations. 
SGVRES represents the sum of all responses from generators that are online and can 
respond in the direction of the frequency error without violating the unit regulation limit. 
In the FBGEN calculation, the value of DBV changes with transitions of the absolute Actual 
Frequency Deviation value (AFD) into the VFBIAS deadband region. The change in the DBV 
value is determined by the transition scalar, PINC. This scalar specifies the change in 
governor response as the frequency deviation continues to be greater than the threshold. 
PINC affects DBV values as follows: 
When absolute AFD is less than the VFBIAS deadband minimum (VFBDB1), then: 
DBV = min (DBVMIN, (DBV - PINC)) 
When absolute AFD exceeds the VFBIAS deadband maximum (VFBDB2), then: 
DBV = max (DBVMAX, (DBV + PINC)) 
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 147 Generation Modeling 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide

3.2.18 TransactingArea 
Transacting areas are companies that can purchase or sell power among themselves. 
Essentially, transacting areas are entities within a host control area that can conduct 
transactions of power. Additional transacting areas can be set up for transactions with 
other host control areas that have not yet been defined. The TransactingArea table is used 
to model a transacting area under a host control area. The ID of a transacting area does 
not need to match the ID of any other component. Each transacting area ID must be unique 
within a host control area. A transacting area does not need to have physical ties with the 
host control area. It is mapped to the TRA record in GENMOM. 
3.2.18.1 Modeling Transaction Areas 
To model transaction areas: 
1. Click Generation on the toolbar and select the Transaction Contracts tree view. 
2. Expand the Host control areas folder to expose its contents. 
– To add a new transaction area record, right-click the Host control area, and select 
the Insert TransactingArea option. 
– To update an existing transaction area record, click its icon. 
3. Model transaction area information in the TransactingArea property sheet. 
3.2.18.2 External Contract Unit Transactions 
The dispatcher can use Unit Commitment (UC) or Hydro-Thermal Coordination (HTC) to 
determine the desired output of external contract units for each hour of the UC study. 
These outputs may then be used to automatically create transaction schedules with the 
external contract units’ host control areas that represent the EMS host control area’s 
portion of the generation, and have not been formally modeled as jointly owned units. This 
capability is primarily used for creating schedules for the Real-Time Generation function. 
External contract units have contracts that limit the level of interchange to multiples of 
blocks or quantitization levels. One or many units may use the same contract. The sum of 
the outputs of the units in a contract must be a multiple of the quantitization amount. For 
each hour of a unit commitment study, the unit outputs are modified to correspond to the 
quantitization levels of the contracts. 
The dispatcher needs to specify the hours of the unit commitment study for which 
schedules are to be created (the specified time must be in the future). At that time, the 
dispatcher invokes the transfer from UC or HTC to the online database. This transfer 
converts the contract unit outputs from UC or HTC into equivalent transaction schedules 
with the contract unit’s host control area. Once the schedules are in the online scheduling 
database, they are treated as any other schedule entered by the dispatcher. 
Transaction type records must be defined for each external contract unit. 
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 149 Generation Modeling 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
3.2.18.3 Transaction Modeling Considerations 
When modeling transactions, consider the following: 
• Keep the number of transaction types to a minimum in the external host control areas. 
• A slave transaction between an external host control area and the EMS OPA can serve 
as the slave to any number of transaction types. The same slave transaction type ID can 
serve all of the transaction types. 
• Normally, in the external system, only one transaction type between host control areas 
is necessary. 
• Costing information is not used for transactions in the external host control areas. 
• Slave transactions are never modeled for the EMS host control area (the area being 
controlled). 
3.2.19 Substation 
The substation is a collection of many components and measurements, such as a 
generator and its MW flow analogs. 
A substation is defined within a host control area, and its name must be globally unique. 
Information about substations is used by all e-terraplatform subsystems: 
e-terratransmission, e-terrascada, e-terrageneration, and e-terrasimulator. It is mapped to 
the PL record in GENMOM. 
3.2.19.1 Modeling Substations 
To model substations: 
1. Click Generation on the toolbar and select the Power Equipment tree view. 
2. Expand the Host Control Areas icon to expose its contents. 
– To model a new substation, right-click the HostControlArea icon under which the 
new substation is to be added and select the Insert Substation option. 
– To update an existing substation, click its icon. 
3. Model substation information in the Substation property sheet. 
4. Map the substation to the appropriate SCADA measurements and controls. 
3.2.20 StartupGroup 
Startup groups specify the number of units at a plant that can be synchronized 
simultaneously in one hour. Startup groups are used only in configurations that implement 
Unit Commitment, the e-terraplatform application for committing and de-committing units. 
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 150 Generation Modeling 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
Startup group records need to be modeled for plants where only a subset of the total 
number of units can be synchronized to the power system in the same hour. 
Startup group IDs must be globally unique. For each startup group, the number of units that 
can be synchronized simultaneously during one hour must be specified (greater than zero). 
It is mapped to the SGROUP record in GENMOM. 
3.2.20.1 Modeling Startup Groups 
To model a startup group: 
1. Click Tables on the toolbar to open the Tables Explorer. 
2. Expand the Generation Other Tables folder. 
3. Click the StartUpGroup icon to display all records in the Grid View. 
– To model a new startup group, enter the EMSName of the new startup group on top 
of the Grid View. Right-click the new record to open its property sheet. Open the 
Associations property group to set association to the substation that the new 
startup group is to be added, and then save your changes. 
– To update an existing startup group, right-click on the record to open its property 
sheet. 
– Model startup group information in the StartUpGroup property sheet. 
3.2.21 ResourceController 
Each substation has one or more resource controllers, which are signaled by AGC to control 
the output of one or more generating units. It is mapped to the PLC record in GENMOM. 
3.2.21.1 PulseCalibration 
AGC uses the Pulse Calibration values to convert the desired PLC error into a control 
command raise/lower pulse. A one-second pulse is equal to a “calibration” MW change 
signal. The PulseCalibration table is used to specify the calibration values used in different 
MW ranges. 
The PulseCalibration table is constructed by entering a series of generation breakpoints 
(MW) that give the Pulse Calibration (MW/sec) at the MW level specified. For MW values 
between breakpoints, the calibration associated with the lower breakpoint is used. 
The Pulse Calibration Raise value must be within the Raise Low Limit and Raise High Limit, 
and the Pulse Calibration Lower value must be within the Lower Low Limit and Lower High 
Limit. The first point of the table must have zero MWs. It is mapped to the CALTBL record in 
GENMOM. 
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 151 Generation Modeling 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
3.2.21.2 Modeling Resource Controllers 
To model resource controllers for a substation: 
1. Click Generation on the toolbar and select the Power Equipment tree view. 
2. Navigate to the Substation icon for the appropriate substation and expand it. 
3. Expand the Resource controllers folder (in the Station Equipment folder) to expose its 
contents. 
– To add a new resource controller record, right-click the Substation icon under which 
new resource controller is to be added and select the Insert ResourceController 
option. 
– To add multiple resource controller records, right-click the Resource controllers 
folder and select the Add Multiple Resource controller option. 
4. Model resource controller information in the Resource controller property sheet. 
5. Map the resource controller to the appropriate SCADA measurements and controls. 
3.2.22 GeneratingUnit 
Generators are components that supply power to the transmission (or distribution) network 
system. A generating unit is a device defined in a substation. When a generating unit is 
defined, its terminal node must be specified. The name of the device must be unique within 
a substation. It is mapped to the UNIT record in GENMOM. 
3.2.22.1 Fuel 
This table is used to define Generation fuel types. It is mapped to the FUEL record in 
GENMOM. 
3.2.22.2 ForbiddenZone 
Generating units with certain physical characteristics have a region of their MW output that 
is not desirable for operation. For hydroelectric units, it can be a region of excessive 
vibration due to cavitation. For thermal units, it can be a region of uneconomical operation 
due to steam turbine valve point loading. These regions are known as forbidden zones, 
prohibited operating zones, gray zones, or disallowed operating ranges. All of these are 
referred to as “forbidden zones” in this document. 
Forbidden zones are defined by their upper and lower bounds. These limits are given in 
gross or net MW, consistent with the other MW values for the unit. 
Each Forbidden Zone record represents a separate forbidden zone. Units without 
telemetered forbidden zone limits can contain multiple Forbidden Zone records. Units with 
telemetered forbidden zone limits can only contain one Forbidden Zone record, a restriction 
enforced during validation. 
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 152 Generation Modeling 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
When multiple Forbidden Zone records exist, their limits must be in ascending order. The 
limits do not need to be confined by the unit economic or LFC limits, but are confined by the 
unit capacity limit. 
Two values can be checked against the forbidden zone limits: unit basepoints and unit 
desired generation. If flags have been set to enforce the forbidden zone limits in the 
Economic Dispatch (ED), unit basepoints are calculated normally and then compared to the 
zone limits. If unit basepoints are found within the forbidden zone, they are adjusted to one 
of the zone limits based on the current generation, the calculated unrestricted limit, and the 
basepoint zone crossing percentage. The basepoint zone crossing percentage is the 
amount of the zone that must be crossed by the basepoint before the adjusted basepoint is 
set to the zone limit, which is opposite the current generation. 
The desired generation for each ResourceController (PLC) is the PLC’s basepoint plus the 
PLC’s regulation component. The desired generation for a PLC with the forbidden zone 
enforcement flag set is checked against the forbidden zones. If the desired generation is not 
in or across a forbidden zone, the PLC is allowed to control the unit normally. If the desired 
generation crosses the forbidden zone, it does not violate the LFC limit, and the time 
between crossings is greater than the minimum time setting, the PLC is allowed to control 
the unit across the zone. If the desired generation is in the forbidden zone, if the desired 
generation is across the zone without the minimum time between the crossing being 
expired, or if the current generation is too far away from the forbidden zone limit, the PLC 
control is limited to the forbidden zone limit closest to the current generation. 
The processing for desired generation related to forbidden zones is effective only for those 
PLCs that have the flag set to enforce forbidden zone restrictions in unit controls. 
An alarm is issued if the PLC is controlling a unit across a forbidden zone, and the AGC or 
the PLC is suspended. An alarm is also issued when the PLC is controlling a unit across a 
forbidden zone, the AGC or PLC is paused, and the time delay for the AGC or PLC to wait 
before entering the suspend state is set to prevent the suspend state. 
The ForbiddenZone class is mapped to the FZONE record in GENMOM. 
3.2.22.3 GrossToNetActivePowerCurve 
This table defines curves that are used to perform gross to net or net to gross conversions 
for measurements for resource controllers, units, and records that are children of units. This 
allows gross and net measurements to be used as alternates for each other. This table is 
mapped to the GRSNET record in GENMOM. 
3.2.22.4 IncrementalHeatRateCurve 
Incremental heat rate curves are modeled for each unit whose generation type defines it as 
economically dispatchable. You construct the curve by entering a series of points that give 
the incremental fuel units (Mega BTU) per MWH at the MW level specified. AGC interpolates 
the points linearly to determine the incremental heat rate at intermediate points. 
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 153 Generation Modeling 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
Incremental heat rate curves must increase monotonically between the minimum 
economic dispatch point and the unit capability. An incremental heat rate curve is never 
extrapolated, and must be defined over the complete range of generation. The first point of 
the curve must occur at zero MWs. 
Each incremental heat rate curve corresponds to a SUBSTATION and UNIT identifier. The 
unit’s incremental heat rate curve is constructed as a series of points, each of which 
specifies the incremental heat in MBTU per MWH that is required to maintain generation at 
a specified MW level. 
It is mapped to the HRATE record in GENMOM. 
3.2.22.4.1 AutoSelectionCriteria 
For units having multiple Incremental Heat Rate Curves (IHRCs), the IHRC in use can be 
selected by the operator or criteria can be defined to support automatic selection. The 
automatic selection is based on any combination of: 
• Time of year 
• Temperature 
• Telemetered status 
• Fuel in use 
This table is used to hold the selection criteria. It is mapped to the HRCRIT record in 
GENMOM. 
3.2.22.5 OperatingShare 
This table is used to define share details for a Jointly Owned Unit (JOU). It is mapped to the 
SHARE record in GENMOM. 
3.2.22.6 WindSpeedCurve 
This table is used to model wind curves. It is mapped to the WCURVE record in GENMOM.

3.2.23 Jointly Owned Units 
Jointly owned units (JOUs) are units owned by more than one host control area, with each 
host control area having its own share of the unit. Share records must be set up for all 
non-physical, internally operated JOUs. 
This section contains background information for modeling JOUs. 
3.2.23.1 JOU Topology 
Three types of PLC-unit combinations are used to represent a single JOU site: 
• Physical Internally Operated JOU: This type has a physical internally operated JOU PLC 
and one physical internally operated JOU unit. This is modeled in the Host control area 
(OPA) that is in control of the JOU and represents the actual unit. 
• Non-Physical Internally Operated JOU: This type is always paired one-to-one with a 
physical internally operated JOU. This type is characterized by a non-physical internally 
operated JOU PLC and a non-physical internally operated JOU unit for each share 
owner. There must be at least two share units under each non-physical PLC, with one of 
these units representing a share belonging to the OPA that is operating the JOU. 
• Externally Operated JOU: This type is represented by a physical externally operated 
JOU PLC and one non-physical externally operated JOU unit. This type is modeled in an 
OPA’s topology when the OPA owns a share of a JOU that is operated by another 
company. 
The topology of internally and externally operated JOUs is illustrated in Figure 46. 
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 155 Generation Modeling 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
 
Figure 46. Topology of JOUs 
Jointly owned units and their PLCs are inserted into the system topology just like other units 
and PLCs. To specify that a PLC and its units are for a jointly owned unit, the PLC’s “JOU?” 
flag is enabled. The Non-Physical flag also must be toggled to the correct value for the PLC 
and its units, depending on which one of the three types of JOUs is being modeled. 
Some requirements to follow about JOU topology are: 
• A physical internally operated JOU must always be followed by its corresponding 
non-physical internally operated JOU. 
• A physical internally operated JOU PLC has one and only one unit; the unit must be a 
physical internally operated JOU. 
• An externally operated JOU PLC has one and only one unit; the unit must be a 
non-physical externally operated JOU. 
• For e-terrasimulator operation, every non-physical internally operated JOU share unit 
belonging to an OPA, other than the operating OPA, has to have a matching externally 
operated JOU modeled in the OPA of the share owner. 
• For e-terrasimulator operation, if an internally operated JOU resides in a non-EMS OPA, 
no matter how many share owners there are, only two shares have to be modeled. 
There should be one share for the EMS OPAs share and one for the JOU operating OPA 
and the rest of the shares. 
• Externally operated JOU PLCs should be toggled so they cannot accept AGC setpoints or 
pulses. This allows a basepoint to be calculated with the PLC status set to “AUT”.

3.2.23.2 JOU Measurement Topology 
Measurement processing and modeling for JOUs is the same as it is for normal units, 
except that the non-physical internally operated JOU representing the operating owner’s 
share has no measurement records. 
 
Figure 47. Data Share for Jointly Owned Units 
3.2.23.3 Modeling Jointly Owned Units 
Most of the data entry for JOUs is done in the same way as it is for normal units. Some 
information required for normal units is not necessary for non-physical internally operated 
units, and will not cause validation errors if omitted. 
Because much of the validation and mapping performed in GMDRIVER is done conditionally 
for JOUs, any errors found in JOU topology or data entry must be corrected before the 
generation model can be validated. The modeler should complete as much of the 
generation operations model as possible before entering JOUs. 
3.2.24 Combined Cycle Unit Modeling 
Traditionally, utilities use gas turbine generators only as a peaker and to support black start 
purposes because of low efficiency and high fuel cost. To improve the overall efficiency of 
gas turbine generator operations, combined cycle groups are established for normal 
operations. A combined cycle group consists of one or more gas turbine generators — each 
with a waste heat generator arranged to supply steam to drive a single steam turbine 
generator as shown in Figure 48. By recovering gas turbine waste heat that otherwise vents 
out to the atmosphere, the overall group efficiency is much improved.

3.2.24.1 ResourceController/GeneratingUnit Modeling Configuration 
Only two ResourceController/GeneratingUnit configurations are supported. 
Configuration 1: Each individual unit in the combined cycle group is associated with a 
ResourceController. 
Configuration 2: All units in the combined cycle group are associated with a single 
ResourceController. 
3.2.24.2 Steam Turbine/Gas Turbine Incremental Heat Rate Curves 
In combined cycle group operations, the amount of heat input to the heat recovery boiler 
depends on the amount of waste heat output from waste heat contributing gas turbines, 
which in turn is related to the total power output from the waste heat contributing gas 
turbine units. Therefore, the incremental heat rate characteristic of the steam turbine in the 
groups can be expressed in terms of total GT output, as depicted in the following diagram. 
Whether a GT Unit is contributing heat depends on the unit heat recovery valve status. 

 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 158 Generation Modeling 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
 
This characteristic is used to derive the composite incremental heat rate curve for the 
group used in Economic Dispatch. 
3.2.24.3 Control Options 
Case 1: Controls for the groups issued to the ST ResourceController. 
In this case, each unit is associated with a separate ResourceController (i.e., modeling 
Configuration 1). When all the gas turbines are contributing heat into the group, the entire 
group is controlled as a single entity and control signals are issued to the ST 
ResourceController. However, in the event that individual GT units opt out of the groups, 
they operate as single cycle units. Control signals to those opted-out GT units are issued to 
their associated RESOURCECONTROLLERs. Controls to the remaining units in the group are 
still issued to the ST ResourceController.  
Case 2: Control issued to the CT ResourceController. 
In this case, controls are issued to individual CT ResourceController within the groups and 
no control is issued to the ST ResourceController. The output of the ST unit simply follows 
the total outputs from the GT units contributing heat to the heat recovery boiler. The ST unit 
in this case is a four steam follower. Individual GT units can opt out of the groups and, as 
such, be controlled as single cycle units. 
Case 3: Control issued to a single ResourceController. 
In this case, regardless of the number of GT units contributing to the combined cycle 
groups, control is issued to one single ResourceController. The resource controller decides 
how to distribute the control received from AGC to the units participating in the groups. 
3.2.25 ConnectingUtility 
A ConnectingUtility is essentially a connected host control area. Therefore, a connecting 
utility must be defined under every host control area with which it has tie lines or tie 
corridors. The identifier assigned to a connecting utility must be unique within a host 
control area. It is mapped to the UTIL record in GENMOM. 

 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 159 Generation Modeling 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
3.2.25.1 Use of ConnectingUtility 
Before any tie corridor relationships can be modeled, the model builder must define a 
ConnectingUtility (UTIL) record under those host control areas that exchange energy. Tie 
corridor (TIE) records will belong to these ConnectingUtility records. The Connecting Utility 
identifier must be unique within each host control area branch of the Connecting Area Tie 
Corridors tree. 
3.2.26 TieCorridor 
A tie corridor is a collection of tie flows that need to be monitored together, either to satisfy 
measurement requirements, or simply because they stretch across a single physical 
corridor (right of way). Tie-line flows are summed to yield the net flow in the tie corridor. 
Tie corridors are modeled by defining two mirror image records for the same tie corridor. 
For example, one tie corridor models the flow from the EMS host control area to an external 
host control area. The other tie corridor models the flow from the external host control area 
to the EMS host control area. Logically, both tie corridors must share the same name. 
A tie corridor consists of one or more tie flows that connect your host control area with 
neighboring areas, including their corresponding accumulators and analogs. This 
information is used by the e-terrageneration and e-terratransmission subsystems and is 
modeled in the e-terrageneration database and propagated to the network data structure 
during network validation by the e-terratransmission subsystem Generation Mapping 
function called GENMAP. 
It is mapped to the TIE record in GENMOM. 
3.2.26.1 Dynamic Load Ties 
A tie corridor may also be a dynamic load tie to support a dynamic schedule between 
operating areas. The dynamic schedule is the sum of all the dynamic load ties, plus any 
Jointly Owned Unit MWs. 
Dynamic load ties have no tie-line records, but require a MW analog measurement record. 
They are used to model the following: 
• Foreign loads that are embedded in the EMS area. 
• EMS load embedded in a neighboring area. 
• EMS generation embedded in a neighboring area. 
Dynamic load ties can also be used to support Joint AGC regulation. 
3.2.26.2 Modeling Connecting Area Tie Corridors 
To model connecting area tie corridors: 
1. Click Generation on the toolbar and select the Connecting Area Tie Corridors tree view. 
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 160 Generation Modeling 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
2. Navigate to the appropriate host control area and expand it. 
3. Model utilities. 
– Add a ConnectingUtility record for every other host control area where there is a tie 
line or tie corridor. 
– Model parameters for the utility in the ConnectingUtility property sheet. 
4. Model connecting area tie corridors under the ConnectingUtility record. 
– Model parameters for the tie corridor in the TieCorridor property sheet. 
– If the connecting tie is not dynamic, no further modeling is needed. 
– If the connecting tie is dynamic, expand the Dynamic Load Tie property group on the 
TieCorridor property sheet. 
– If the connecting tie is both dynamic and for Joint AGC, add Joint AGC information 
by expanding the respective Joint AGC Requester Information and Joint AGC 
Supplier Information property groups. 
5. Map tie lines and tie corridors to the appropriate SCADA measurements and controls. 
3.2.27 TieFlow 
A tie flow, used to model tie-lines, must be modeled for each physical line in the EMS that 
spans between AGC host control areas. It is mapped to the TYLN record in GENMOM. 
3.2.27.1 Connecting Area Tie Corridors and Tie Lines 
A tie line is mapped to the TieFlow record in e-terrasource. The model builder defines the 
initial line topology using the AC Transmission Lines property sheet, and then replicates 
those lines that are tie lines in the Generation model using the Connecting Area Tie 
Corridors property sheet. Once the data model is exported to the Network database, 
NETMOM, the model builder invokes the Network-Generation Mapping Validation function, 
GENMAP, to propagate the tie line model back to NETMOM. GENMAP creates TLN records 
and inserts them in NETMOM under their assigned AREA record.  
3.2.27.2 Model an AC Transmission Line as a Member of a TieCorridor 
1. Click Generation on the toolbar and select the Connecting Area Tie Corridors tree view. 
2. Navigate to the connecting host control area of interest and expand it. 
3. Model the connecting electric utilities, as follows: 
– Identify the HostControlArea that is connected by tie corridors and tie lines. 
– Add a ConnectingUtility record under these HostControlAreas by right-clicking on a 
HostControlArea and selecting Insert ConnectingUtility; one ConnectingUtility for 
each host control area connection that will be modeled. 
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 161 Generation Modeling 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
– Identify each utility on a ConnectingUtility property sheet by clicking on the 
ConnectingUtility icon. 
Note: The modeler can specify that the utility delivers power to itself over a tie line 
(Internal Tie Line). 
4. Model tie corridors under the ConnectingUtility record by inserting TieCorridor records. 
Right-click and select the Insert TieCorridor option on the pop-up menu. 
5. Model tie corridor details about the Connecting Area Tie Corridor property sheet by 
specifying the TieCorridor record ID, the connecting company, and the operating 
parameters for bulk power exchange. Entering an association with a Geographical 
Region (i.e., connecting company) is optional. 
Note 1: This is one of a mirrored-pair of TieCorridor records that the model builder 
must create. The tie lines in these paired TieCorridor records have the same name and 
tie line (TieFlow) specification. The other member in the mirrored-pair must reside 
under the other utility that is party to the bulk power exchange. 
The model builder must match the identifiers in these ACLine entries with those used 
to specify tie lines in the tie corridors (Connecting Area Tie Corridor property sheet). 
Note 2: Internal ties do not require a mirrored-pair. 
Note 3: Dynamic load ties do not require tie lines (TieFlow records). 
6. Model a dynamic load tie by setting the Dynamic Tie field to Yes. Dynamic load ties do 
not have Tie Line (TieFlow) children. 
7. If the tie corridor is both for dynamic load monitoring and for Joint-AGC operations, 
expand the Dynamic Load Tie property group and add Requester- or Supplier-specific 
Joint AGC information. 
8. Model tie line details about the Lines in Corridor tab of the Connecting Area Tie Corridor 
property sheet as follows (does not apply to dynamic load tie corridor modeling): 
– Right-click on the TieCorridor and select Insert TieFlow. 
– Specify the Tie Line ID in the EMSName field under the Identification property group. 
This value must be duplicated in the mirrored-pair specification. 
– Specify the association to the terminal at which tie line measurements are taken. 
– If the tie line is a transformer, set the “Is a Line?” field to No. 
– If the tie line measurement is taken in the parent host control area, change the “In 
this OPA?” field to Yes. Switch the mirrored-pair flag of this type to No. 
9. Map tie lines and tie corridors to SCADA measurements and controls using the 
Generation Telemetry View. 
10. Save your changes. 
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 162 Generation Modeling 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
3.2.28 PLCState 
This table is used to define the operating states of a PLC (e.g., offline, on automatic control, 
regulating, etc.). It is mapped to the STPLC record in GENMOM. 
3.2.29 PLCStateGroup 
This table is used to define groups under a PLC state. It is mapped to the STGRP record in 
GENMOM. 
3.2.30 PLCStateElement 
The PLC state model consists of a number of states. The model can be designed such that a 
PLC can match multiple states at the same time, or only a single state. Each state must 
have one or more groups, and each group must have one or more elements. An element 
consists of a flag (e.g., AUT_PLC) and an indication of whether the flag needs to be True or 
False to match. Global flags and flags on the PLC or OPA records can be used for elements. 
This model is mapped to the STELE record in GENMOM.

GenOrder is a property defined on most of the GENMOM related entities in e-terrasource,

• AgcPauseSuspendCriteria (PSTEMP)

• Fuel (FUEL) 
• GeneratingUnit (UNIT) 
• GenerationByType (GTY) (Note 1) 
• GenerationType (GTYPE)

• InadvertentAccount (INAD) 
• InadvertentDay (DAYS) 
• InadvertentProfile (INADPF) 
• IncrementalHeatRateCurve (HRATE) 
• Market (MARKET) 
• MarketType (MARTYP) 
• OperatingShare (SHARE)

• PLCStateElement (STELE) 
• PLCStateGroup (STGRP) 
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 164 Generation Modeling 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
• ResourceController (PLC) 
• ResourceStatus (RESSTA) 
• StartUpGroup (SGROUP) 
• Substation (PL) 
• TelemetryDisplayGroup (ZDISGP) 
• TelemetryInput (ZIN) 
• TelemetryMapping (ZMAP) 
• TelemetryOutput (ZOUT) 
• TelemetryTemplate (ZTEMP) 
• TieCorridor (TIE) 
• TieFlow (TYLN) 
• TransactingArea (TRA) 
• WindSpeedCurve (WCURVE)  
The GenOrder property is used to determine how a GENMOM record is ordered with respect 
to its parent record in GENMOM during an e-terrasource EMS Export. The GenOrder 
property serves two purposes: to retain the order in which records are ordered in GENMOM 
during an e-terrasource roundtrip, and to allow customers to specify where a record is 
located in GENMOM when its mapped record is manually created in e-terrasource. The 
GenOrder property is manually entered for new records created in e-terrasource. 
The GenOrder property has two validation requirements: 
• It is designated as a required field, such that any GenOrder property with a null value is 
caught during “Check Required Fields Validation”. 
• In a record, it is validated to ensure its uniqueness with respect to its parent record.  
For non-hierarchical records in GENMOM, such as EMPFuelType (FUELTY), validation rules (in 
this case EMPFT_GenOrder_Unique) are defined in the metamodel and are invoked during 
Generation Model validation.  
For hierarchical records in GENMOM, such as GeneratingUnit (UNIT), validation rules are 
defined in SQL procedures and are executed during “GenOrder WRT Parent Unique” 
validation. 
Note: The GenerationByType (GTY) record is only supported in e-terraplatform 3.0 and 
later versions. 
3.4 Generation Alarms Model 
Generation alarms can be issued by various tasks, as specified in the data structure set up 
by a programmer/engineer. 
The following three components must be considered when defining Generation alarms: 
• Alarm characteristic definition in GENMODEL 
• Alarm specification in the ALARM Database 
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 165 Generation Modeling 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
• Alarm format picture definitions in RTGEN.ALMMSG 
The request to issue an alarm originates in RTGEN, using the data defined in GENMODEL. 
The Alarm application uses ALARM database data to process the application and display 
the corresponding message defined in RTGEN.ALMMSG. 
How a Generation alarm is configured depends on whether the alarm needs to be 
acknowledged individually, acknowledged as part of a group, or simply shown on the 
System Activity Log (SYSACT). 
• Alarms that need to be acknowledged individually must be set up with a one-to-one 
relationship between the GENMODEL definition and the ALARM database definition. 
• Alarms that need to be acknowledged as a group, but not individually, must be set up 
using one of the following methods: 
– Grouping alarm exceptions under an OBJDEF record in the ALARM database defined 
for group acknowledgement. Normally, this is the preferred approach. 
– Assigning the same alarm exception ID (from the ALARM database) to more than one 
Generation alarm. 
• Operator entry logging alarms are simply logged in SYSACT. 
For detailed information about ALARM database definitions and procedures, refer to the 
Alarm User’s Guide. 
3.4.1 GenAlarmConfiguration

Proprietary – See Copyright Page 166 Generation Modeling 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide

3.6 Reserve Monitor Model 
The Generalized Reserve Monitor (RESMON) function in e-terrageneration calculates 
customer defined reserve quantities using a table driven approach. In this approach, the 
reserve categories, corresponding available reserve calculation equations, reserve 
requirement calculation equations, reserve alarms, and different summation records are 
defined in the reserve model definition. Real-time RESMON processing does the calculation 
for each reserve type and issues alarms if necessary. The output data is saved in common 
two-dimensional arrays in the RESMOM database in e-terrahabitat; these two-dimensional 
output arrays are shown in analyst displays.  
Through the generalized approach, the reserve monitor function is easily modifiable by 
making changes to the reserve model definition rather than the code. For customers, it is 
easier to maintain and more flexible to use.  
e-terrasource provides full modeling capability to support real-time Reserve Monitor 
functionality. Within e-terrasource, a modeler can create, delete, and modify all modeler-
configurable Reserve Monitor records. The Reserve Monitor model can then be exported to 
an e-terrahabitat modeling clone for final validation and then uploaded to a real-time 
clone.  
A modeler may select various resources for contributing to different reserves, such as DC 
ties, hydro units equipped with high-set under-frequency relays, interruptible loads, etc. 
Reserve contributors are defined as ResContributor (CTRB) records. A flag provided on each 
contributor (e.g., UNIT) indicates whether this contribution can be toggled online to 
contribute or not contribute to the reserve. 
The generalized approach allows reserve requirements to be applied at any level. For each 
modeled reserve requirement, there are indirect pointers to the records for which the 
requirement is calculated. A selectable “Replaceable” flag is provided for each reserve 
requirement. When enabled, the reserve requirement may be modified online (note that this 
is unlikely if the reserve requirement is dynamically calculated, a capability RESMON 
provides). 
RESMON outputs an alarm when there is a shortfall of reserves. A return-to-normal alarm is 
issued when the reserve deficiency disappears. RESMON allows repeating deficiency 
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 172 Generation Modeling 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
alarms, and the frequency is definable. Support is also provided to issue additional alarms if 
the available reserve of a given class continues to drop. The modeled characteristics of 
these alarms are configured in e-terrasource. 
In addition to tracking by type (e.g., spinning), customer reserves are typically tracked over 
physically distinct zones (e.g., OPAs and PLs). With the generalized approach, this is handled 
by the proper modeling of reserves. For each contributor there is a ResSummation record 
that defines the records to which that contribution should be added. For example, one kind 
of contributor is UNIT, and contributions from UNIT are often summed to the OPA level.  
The e-terrageneration Reserve Monitor (RESMON) function includes: 
• A generalized reserve definition library and reserve calculation library that is validated 
by the modeling code. 
• Generalized reserve real-time processing, which includes reserve and reserve 
requirement calculation and generating alarms. 
• A generalized display for reserve value and reserve requirement. It also allows online 
entries of some parameters. 
• Multiple reserve thresholds are processed and alarmed. Each alarm threshold has an 
independent user-modifiable repeat period and deadband.  
Table 3 shows how the RESMOM Record Types in e-terrahabitat map to their corresponding 
table names in the e-terrasource relational database. In e-terrasource, record types are 
called metaEntities, and records are called Entities.

The following sections describe the major components and steps to construct a Reserve 
Monitor (RESMON) Model. 
3.6.1 General Discussion of Modeling the Reserve Monitor  
The Reserve Monitor tree view is the main location to perform modeling tasks in 
e-terrasource. A high level screenshot is provided below. 
 
Figure 52. Reserve Display Group Definition 
At a high level, the Reserve Monitor defines reserve types and monitors real-time 
contributions to each type of reserve, notifying operators when contributions are 
insufficient to meet requirements (if there are indeed requirements to be met). When 
beginning to understand the Reserve Monitor model from the e-terrasource perspective, it 
is useful to focus first on Reserve Type and related records. 
Each of the folders in the tree view can be expanded to reveal a hierarchy of entity types 
representing the Reserve Monitor model. While each are explained in detail in following 
sections, overview descriptions are provided below. 

 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 174 Generation Modeling 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
The Reserve Type tree 
The Reserve Type tree is useful as a starting place to understand the model, since this is 
where the heart of the model is defined. In other words, it is difficult to understand the 
purpose of other Reserve Monitor model entities without first understanding the basic 
purpose of those contained in the Reserve Type tree. 
The Reserve Type entity and all of its descendant entities in the tree view can be 
understood as a template for reserve calculations that users may want to implement in 
their systems. Reserve Type entities and descendant entities define the character and 
behavior of reserve calculations, referencing other parts of the model to assist in this 
definition.  
The Reserve Display Group tree 
Reserve Display Group entities are referenced by children of Reserve Type entities to define 
the display characteristics. The Reserve Display Group entity type exists solely to define the 
display properties of records used in the Reserve Monitor model. 
The Reserve Expression tree 
The Reserve Expression library is also referenced by various entities in the Reserve Type 
tree to define the conditions and calculations used in the Reserve Monitor model. The 
Reserve Expression tree is simply a math library to be referenced by the rest of the Reserve 
Monitor model entities. 
The Host Control Area tree 
The Host Control Area tree expands to show the modeled Host Control Areas. This is the 
tree view location where the defined Reserve Types can be assigned to specific Host Control 
Areas where the reserve calculations should apply. The implementation of a Reserve Type 
on a specific Host Control Area is called a Reserve Category for that Host Control Area. 
Without the Reserve Category, no reserve monitoring would take place since the defined 
reserve types would not apply to any modeled Host Control Area. Inserting new records on 
this branch is the last step when adding a new reserve to the model. 
The Reserve Monitor Parameters tree 
The Reserve Monitor Parameters tree holds the reserve configuration properties – a table 
with a single row that defines global configuration options. It corresponds to the RESMOM 
ITEMS table. 
3.6.1.1 Real-Time Processing 
In real-time processing, the reserve from each contributor is calculated. Special processing 
may be coded if the reserve calculation is very complex (although, this is a project related 
custom). Then the reserve is accumulated as pre-defined. Reserve from all contributors is 
summed for comparing with the reserve requirement.  
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 175 Generation Modeling 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
The reserve requirement is calculated in real time. An alarm is issued if there is a shortage. 
Operators are allowed to overwrite the reserve requirement if needed. Alarm deadband 
(percent of the reserve requirement) is applied to screen the return-to-normal alarm. 
3.6.1.2 Export from e-terrasource 
After RESMOM is exported from e-terrasource, RESMOM validation is executed. During 
RESMOM validation in e-terrahabitat, two two-dimensional arrays are created to save the 
available reserve values and the requirement values. Reserve display types define the 
structure of these arrays and provide the base labels for the rows. 
3.6.2 Preparation 
Prior to building the Reserve Model, the RESMON analyst should: 
1. Determine the reserve quantities that need to be monitored. For example, spinning 
reserve or operating reserve. These are the reserve types in the model.  
2. Determine if any of the reserve values need to be exported to other databases, 
applications, or non-RESMON displays. 
3. Determine which reserve quantities need to be reported at the Operating Area level.  
4. Determine if any of these quantities need to be placed directly on the Generation Area 
Status display. 
5. Determine the calculations required to produce these quantities. These are the reserve 
expressions used in the model. 
6. Determine which record types are used for the reserve expressions and reserve types. 
These are used to define the reserve display groups. 
7. Determine which reserve types have specific numeric requirements and alarm 
conditions. These are used to define the reserve requirements and reserve alarms.  
8. Determine if any of the requirement values need to be exported to other databases, 
applications, or non-RESMON displays. 
3.6.3 Basic Steps for e-terrasource Modeling 
It may be helpful for users who are new to e-terrasource to reference this brief step-by-step 
guide for modeling in e-terrasource. This is not meant as a substitute for training to use the 
e-terrasource product, but may help to refresh the memory of those who have already 
completed the training but lack experience, or are unfamiliar with the Reserve Monitor in 
e-terrasource. 
1. Click Generation on the toolbar and select the Reserve Monitor tree view.  
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 176 Generation Modeling 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
 
2. Expand the Reserve Monitor icon to expose its contents. 
 
3. To insert a new entity, right-click on the desired folder icon or parent record and select 
Insert from the context menu. 
 

 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 177 Generation Modeling 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
4. Create associations and enter property details on the property sheet for the new entity. 
5. Existing entities may be modified or deleted in a similar fashion via the Tree View and 
property sheets. 
6. Save your changes. Remember that an active project is necessary in order to save 
changes. 
7. Run the Reserve Monitor validation to determine whether you have omitted any critical 
fields or violated other validation rules. 
3.6.4 Modeling Reserve Display Groups 
A Reserve Display Group (ResDisplayGroup) is a representation of a group of like records in 
the source database (e.g., plants or units). The Display Group allows the analyst to control 
the order in which records of a given type are processed by RESMON. For example, the 
internal tables could be oriented to process records in hierarchical order, by parent, or all at 
once (for a source type that is non-hierarchical). 
Examples of some of the display objects that are typically modeled in RESMON are:  
• Operating Areas 
• Tie lines 
• Plants  
• Plant Controllers 
• Units 
Figure 53 shows a screenshot of the Reserve Display Group representation in e-terrasource. 
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 178 Generation Modeling 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
 
Figure 53. Reserve Display Group Definition 
The following properties are defined through this property sheet, organized in the property 
groups shown: 
• Identification 
– Description: An optional character string used to identify the Display Group on other 
reserve model displays. 
• Generation > Reserve Monitor function 
– Target Database: A character string to identify the source e-terrahabitat database. 
– Target Record: A character string to identify the source e-terrahabitat record in the 
source database. 
– Special Processing: A character string to specify any special processing to be 
performed when validation builds the two-dimensional matrix. Currently only 
“UNITPHYS” (relative to Jointly Owned Units) is supported. 
– Indentation: Number of spaces to indent the entry label on the reserve displays. This 
is a menu selection ranging from NONE (zero) to five (5) spaces. 
– Previous Display Group: If this entry defines a new record group (e.g., the first 
display group to reference Plant records), this value should be set to null. If this is a 

 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 179 Generation Modeling 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
sub-entry under a previous display group, this value should point to the immediately 
preceding previous display group of the same type.  
– Display Mode: Method to use when including the records associated with a display 
group. This menu selection is only available for the top level of a given display group 
(i.e., an entry whose “Previous Display Group” is set to zero). 
∗ All at once: Process all possible entries the first time they are encountered. This 
selection completely ignores any hierarchical relationships. 
∗ By Parent: Process all possible entries for a given parent when encountered. 
Similar records under different parent records will not be processed. This 
selection allows records that have indirect (I$parent_child) definitions to be 
included in the expected table location. 
∗ Hierarchy: Process only those records who are hierarchical descendants of the 
preceding display group. This selection allows records that have indirect 
(I$parent_child) definitions to be included in the expected table location. 
3.6.5 Modeling Reserve Types 
The Reserve Type entity and all of its descendant entities in the Tree View can be 
understood as a template for reserve calculations that users may want to implement in 
their systems. The template is first defined by creating Reserve Type entities and 
descendant entities as needed: ResContributor, ResCondition, ResExpressionRef, 
ResConstraint, ResSummation, ResSumConstraint, ResSumCondition, ReserveReq, and 
ReserveReqAlarm are all the descendants of ReserveType and make up the bulk of Reserve 
Monitor entity types. This template can then be applied to a particular Host Control Area by 
creating a Reserve Category entity that contains associations with both the Host Control 
Area (its parent in the hierarchical structure) and the desired Reserve Type. The distinction 
between a Reserve Type and Reserve Category exists so that a given reserve calculation 
can be applied selectively to some Host Control Areas, but not others. 
When designing a Reserve Type, the analyst must determine which Reserve Types need to 
be represented and the detailed calculation behavior of these Reserve Types. For example, 
a utility might decide that spinning, operating, or other reserve-related quantities need to 
be monitored locally, but be obligated to provide additional performance values to an ISO 
or RTO for reporting purposes. In terms of implementing the design in e-terrasource, most 
of the key characteristics of the Reserve Type are represented as properties and 
associations on the descendant entities, not the Reserve Type entity itself. The first step in 
creating a complete Reserve Type in the model is simply to insert a new ReserveType record 
and choose an appropriate EMS name.  
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 180 Generation Modeling 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
 
Figure 54. Modeled Reserve Types 
The following Reserve Type properties are defined through the appropriate property sheets, 
organized by the property groups shown: 
ReserveType record 
• Identifiers 
– EMS Name: A character string to identify the Reserve Type. This ID is entered in the 
corresponding Reserve Category fields to associate the reserve type with a 
particular HostControlArea. This ID is used for all internally mapping of the reserve 
type (i.e., “Label”). 
• Identifiers > Optional Identifiers 
– Description: A character string description documenting the purpose of the reserve 
type. This field is not used for any other purpose. 
• Generation > Reserve Monitor function 
– Label: A character string to identify the Reserve Type on operator displays. If this 
field is blank, the RESMON validation program assigns it the same value as the 
Reserve Type ID. The chief intent of this field is to allow multiple reserve types that 
produce quantities the operators view as equivalent, but which are actually the 

 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 181 Generation Modeling 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
result of different calculations. For example, reserve types ID=”EMP_SPIN” and 
ID=“PJM_SPIN” are both labeled as LABEL=“SPINNING”. 
– Use in AGC?: This flag indicates that a given calculation is valid for use in AGC 
processing (either DTS or real time). If this flag is set to No, the reserve type is not 
processed for AGC and no reserve requirements may be defined for it.  
– Use in STGEN?: This flag indicates that a given calculation is valid for use in STGEN 
processing. If this flag is set to No, the reserve type is not processed for STGEN.  
3.6.6 Modeling Reserve Contributors  
Reserve contributors define the lowest-level entity (lowest level in the hierarchical database 
sense) on which reserves of this Reserve Type are to be monitored. For example, a UNIT 
may be the lowest level contributor for a Reserve Type associated with a PLC or PLANT. For 
each contributor, the analyst can specify the reserve expressions used to calculate the 
reserve value (e.g., available capacity), the conditions when a given value is processed (e.g., 
only if UNIT is online), and any reserve constraints (e.g., limiting total contribution). These 
entries are made from the Reserve Contributor folder on the Reserve Monitor navigation 
tree as shown below. 
 
Figure 55. Reserve Contributor 

 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 182 Generation Modeling 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
The following records may be inserted and modified in the Reserve Contributor sub-tree: 
• Reserve Contributor (ResContributor) 
• Reserve [Contributor] Condition (ResCondition) 
• Reserve [Contributor] Constraint (ResConstraint) 
The following properties are defined through the appropriate property sheets, organized by 
the property groups shown: 
ResContributor record: 
• Associations 
– Reserve Display Group: This is the association to the Reserve Display Group, which 
will drive this contributor. 
• Generation > Reserve Monitor function 
– Enable online contribution selection?: This flag indicates that the reserve 
contribution may be toggled by the operator at runtime. The toggle is visible on the 
RESMON_AVAILABLE_DETAILS display. If this flag is not set, the option is not visible 
on the runtime display. 
– Export: The Export flag indicates that the reserve contribution should be exported 
(back) to the source record. When this flag is set to Yes, the export field becomes 
enterable. 
– Field Name for Export: This is a character string definition of the field where the 
contribution will be written. The Field Name is not enterable unless the Export flag is 
set to Yes. 
ResCondition record: 
• Associations 
– Reserve Expression: This is the association to the reserve condition expression to be 
evaluated to “enable” this contribution. If the expression returns a TRUE (non-zero) 
value, the associated reserve value is processed. A result of FALSE (zero) causes the 
value to be skipped.  
Note: Processing for each individual contributor stops with the first condition that 
resolves to TRUE. Even if subsequent conditions are also satisfied, only the first is used. 
• Generation > Reserve Monitor function 
– Invert?: If the argument is Integer or Real, this flag indicates that it will be 
arithmetically negated (plus to minus).  
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 183 Generation Modeling 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
ResExpressionRef record: 
• Associations 
– Value Expression: This is the association of the reserve value expression that yields 
the reserve contribution. 
• Generation > Reserve Monitor function 
– Use Absolute Value?: When set, the value is changed to the absolute value. 
– Negate Value?: If Boolean, the value of this argument will be logically negated (i.e., 
true to false). 
ResConstraint record (Optional): 
• Associations 
– Reserve Expression: This is the association to the reserve constraint expression, 
which yields the reserve limit value. 
• Generation > Reserve Monitor function 
– Constraint Type: This menu selection indicates whether the constraint is imposing 
either a maximum (“Max Limit”) or minimum (“MinLimit”) limit on the reserve 
contribution. 
– Use Absolute Value?: When set, the value of this element is changed to the absolute 
value. 
– Negated?: If Boolean, the value of this argument will be logically negated (i.e., true to 
false).

to the source record. When this flag is set to Yes, the export field becomes enterable. 
– Field Name for Export: This is a character string definition of the GENMOM field

e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide

reserve violation alarm. Set to “-1” if no repeat is required. 
– Deadband: The amount by which the reserve value must return before the alarm 
condition is cleared. Expressed as an absolute value in percent (unitless). Set to zero 
if no deadband is required. 
– Threshold Type: Defines whether the threshold for this alarm is a maximum 
threshold or minimum threshold (that is, whether the alarm will be triggered when 
the monitored value goes above the threshold or below the threshold). In general, 
reserve alarms will have Threshold Type “Min Limit”, meaning that the alarm is 
triggered when the available reserve drops below the required reserve. 
3.6.9 Assigning Reserve Types to a Reserve Area 
Once reserve types are determined, it is a simple matter to indicate which of these values 
should be processed for a given Reserve Area and which should be available on the 
Generation Area Status display. Normally only those values of critical importance to the 
operators are “promoted” in this fashion. The operator still has the option to access the 
Reserve Summary display or the Reserve Available Details display for a more complete list. 
Note that only the OPA level quantities can be exported in this manner. 
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 188 Generation Modeling 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
When using e-terrasource, the modeler should keep in mind that the standard 
e-terrageneration product displays only the first eight (8) reserve types assigned to any 
given OPA. The standard e-terrageneration database schema is limited to twenty (20) 
reserve types per OPA. The standard displays may be modified (using Display Builder) if 
additional reserve types need to be displayed on the main displays. RESMON issues a 
warning if no reserve types are selected for a control center OPA.

3.6.10 Modeling Reserve Expressions 
The reserve expression library models simple mathematical calculations. It contains 
expression (REXP in RESMOM, ReserveExpression in e-terrasource) and expression element 
(RELE in RESMOM, ReserveOperation in e-terrasource) records. Each expression element 
can be either an operand or an operator. The operators may be simple math operators (e.g., 
+, *), logical operators (e.g., AND, NOR), comparison tests (e.g., EQ, GT), or simple math 
functions (e.g., EXP, LOG). The operand is allowed to be an external database field, a 
character string, an integer, a real number, or another expression. Unary operations such 
as ABS (absolute value), NEG (negate), and NOT (logical negation) are allowed on each 
operand. RESMOM validation in e-terrahabitat ensures the correctness of the expression. 
The reserve expression library allows the analyst to model simple mathematical 
calculations. Each expression is entered as a sequence of elements. Each element can be 
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 190 Generation Modeling 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
either an operand (e.g., a constant or a data field) or an operator (e.g., a math operator or 
function). 
There are several distinct groups of operators:  
• Simple math operators (+, -, *, /) always yield a floating point result. 
• Comparisons (EQ, LE, LT, GE, GT, NE) always yield a 1=TRUE, or 0=FALSE result. These 
may be used on either numeric or string arguments. 
• Logical operators (AND, NAND, NOR, OR) always yield a 1=TRUE, or 0=FALSE result. 
• Math functions (MAX, MIN, LOG, EXP) always yield a floating point result. 
Operands are allowed to be an external database field, a character string, an integer, a real 
number, or another reserve expression. Unary operations such as ABS (absolute value), NEG 
(negate), and NOT (logical negation) are allowed on each operand. Note that it is illegal to 
combine the unary NOT operator with any other unary operators. 
Operations are entered in standard algebraic form (i.e., OPERAND OPERATOR OPERAND). For 
example: A*B, A max B. LOG is implemented as “LOG Y of X”. EXP is implemented as “X to the 
Y power” (note that a square root is X to the 0.5 power). 
Parentheses are not currently supported. However, any given expression may reference 
(nest) another expression to accomplish the same result. For example, the expression 
“D=A*(B + C)” can be modeled as “A*E”, where E is the expression “E=B+C”. 
All reserve expressions are listed alphabetically under the Reserve Expression folder on the 
Reserve Monitor navigation tree. 
  
Figure 59. Reserve Expressions 

 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 191 Generation Modeling 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide

3.6.12 Controlling the Order of Exported RESMOM Records 
SortOrder is a property defined on most of the RESMOM related entities in e-terrasource, 
listed below:  
• ResCategory (RCAT) 
• ResCondition (COND) 
• ResConstraint (RLIM) 
• ResContributor (CTRB) 
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 195 Generation Modeling 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
• ResDisplayGroup (RDISP) 
• ResSumConition (SCOND) 
• ResSumConstraint (SLIM) 
• ResSummation (SUMIN)) 
• ReserveExpression (REXP) 
• ReserveOperation (RELE) 
• ReserveReq (RREQ) 
• ReserveReqAlarm (RALM) 
• ReserveType (RTYP)  
The SortOrder property is used to determine how a RESMOM record is ordered with respect 
to its parent record in RESMOM during an e-terrasource EMS Export. The SortOrder property 
serves two purposes: to retain the order in which records are ordered in RESMOM during an 
e-terrasource roundtrip, and to allow customers to specify where a record is located in 
RESMOM when its mapped record is manually created in e-terrasource. The SortOrder 
property is manually entered for new records created in e-terrasource. 
The SortOrder property on these records is designated as a required field such that any 
SortOrder property with a null value is caught during “Check Required Fields Validation”.  
3.7 Generation Model Validation Rules 
Many of the generation model validation rules are implemented in the attribute and 
association definitions of the metadata entity such as data range, string length, and 
association cardinality. Those generation model rules are enforced during data entry. In 
addition to those, rules are defined in the generation validation modules, which are only 
triggered during workspace validation as part of full workspace validation and generation 
model validation. 
While there are many generation validation rules defined in the metadata, these rules fall 
into just a few categories. Instead of listing each and every validation rule, this section 
describes the general form and function of generation validation rules, including rule types, 
naming conventions, and entity abbreviations. Finally, this section concludes with a note on 
non-null validation. 
3.7.1 Generation Validation Rule Types 
Table 4 lists and describes the generation model validation rule types. 
 
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 196 Generation Modeling 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
Table 4. Generation Validation Rule Types and Descriptions 
Rule Type Rule Description 
Unique Checks that the property ha s a unique value compared to other 
entities of the same type. For example, 
InadvProfile_GenOrder_Unique issues an error message if two or 
more InadvertentProfile entities have the same value for their 
GenOrder property. 
InOrder Checks that the two values lis ted are in the proper order. A common 
use for this validation rule type is to validate that a maximum limit 
property is greater than a minimum limit property. For example, 
PC_MaxMin_LowerPulseCal_InOrder issues an error message if the 
property MaxLowerPulseCal is less than the property 
MinLowerPulseCal on a PulseCalibration entity. 
WithinBound Checks that a property is with in the bounds set by other properties or 
constants. The validation error message specifies the bounds.  
NonNull Checks that a property is not null. 
Validation rule non-null checks are useful when the non-null check is 
conditional upon some other modeled value. For example, 
GU_GenOrder_NonNull issues an error if the GenOrder property on a 
Generating Unit entity is null, but only if the ForGeneration flag on 
that Generating Unit is also true. For more information about non-
null validation, see section 3.7.4 Note on Non-Null Validation. 
AboveMins Checks that a property is gr eater than two other properties. This 
would be used in case it is not certain which of the other two 
properties might be greater than the other. As of e-terrasource 3.0, 
only one generation validation rule has this type, 
STN_AbsMaxCombDisch_AboveMins. 
3.7.2 Generation Model Validation Rules Naming Convention 
Generation validation rule names follow a semi-standardized naming convention. 
Validation rules from other domains do not necessarily follow this convention; for example, 
network validation rules follow a similar convention but omit the entity abbreviation from 
the validation rule name. 
The generation validation rule naming convention is: 
[EntityAbbreviation]_[PropertyName(s)]_[ValidationRuleType] 
For example, consider the rule named GU_GenOrder_NonNull: 
• GU is an abbreviation for Generating Unit. This validation rule applies to Generating Unit 
entities. 
 
Proprietary – See Copyright Page 197 Generation Modeling 
e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide 
• GenOrder is a property defined on the Generating Unit. This validation rule involves the 
GenOrder property. 
• NonNull is the validation check that is performed on the GenOrder property on 
GeneratingUnit entities. 
Some validation rules do not precisely follow this convention, but it is a good rule of thumb. 
The “InOrder” rule type follows a slightly different convention. If the two properties that 
should be in order are called MaxLimit and MinLimit, for example, the name of the 
validation rule is [EntityAbbreviation]_MaxMin_Limit_InOrder. From a design perspective, 
this was done in order to enable standardized validation error messages for common 
InOrder validation rules.
